en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Mahāvagga 1.
Mahākhandhaka (The Great Chapter)
1. The Discourse on Awakening Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the foot of the Bodhi tree, having just attained full awakening for the first time.
Then the Blessed One sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
Then, during the first watch of the night, the Blessed One attended to dependent origination in direct and reverse order:

"With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition..."
The six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases arises contact; conditioned by contact arises feeling; conditioned by feeling arises craving;
conditioned by craving arises clinging; conditioned by clinging arises existence; conditioned by existence arises birth;
conditioned by birth arise aging and death, as well as sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
But from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations; from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness;
from the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; from the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases. From the cessation of the six sense bases...
With the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, the cessation of craving;
with the cessation of craving, the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, the cessation of birth;
and with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
“Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“When phenomena truly become manifest...”
For the brahmin who meditates with ardor,
all his doubts vanish when he understands phenomena along with their causes.
Then, during the middle watch of the night, the Blessed One attended to dependent origination in forward and reverse order:
"With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises...
Thus there is the arising of this entire mass of suffering... [and so on]..."
“...there is cessation.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:
“When, indeed, phenomena become manifest...”
For the brahmin who meditates with ardor,
all his doubts vanish once he has realized the destruction of the conditions.
Then, during the last watch of the night, the Blessed One directed his mind to dependent origination in forward and reverse order:
“With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises … [and so on] … such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering …” [and so on].
“...there is cessation.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired utterance:
“When, indeed, phenomena become manifest...”
For the brahmin who meditates with ardor,
dispelling the army of Māra,
he stands like the sun illuminating the sky.
The Discourse on Awakening is concluded.
2. The Discourse on the Cowherd.
Then, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and [departed] from the foot of the Bodhi tree.
He went to where the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree was, and having arrived, he sat at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree for seven days in a single cross-legged posture,
experiencing the bliss of liberation.
Then a certain brahmin of a grumbling disposition approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side.
Standing there, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:
“In what way, Master Gotama, is one a brahmin, and what are the qualities that make one a brahmin?
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“The brahmin who has banished evil qualities...”
One who is free from impurity, self-controlled,
who has reached the end of knowledge and lived the holy life—
he alone may rightfully utter the Brahma-word.
“He for whom there is no conceit anywhere in the world.
The Discourse on the Cowherd is finished. 3.
The Discourse on Mucalinda.
Then, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and went from the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree to the Mucalinda tree.
Having arrived, he sat for seven days at the foot of the Mucalinda tree in a single cross-legged posture,
experiencing the bliss of liberation.
Now at that time, a great unseasonable storm arose, with torrential rain for seven days, cold winds, and overcast skies.
Then Mucalinda, the king of the nāgas, emerged from his own abode, coiled his body around the Blessed One’s body seven times, and stood above his head spreading a great hood, thinking:
“May there be no cold for the Blessed One; may there be no heat for the Blessed One; may there be no contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, or creeping things for the Blessed One.”
Then, at the end of seven days, the Naga king Mucalinda, perceiving that the sky was clear and free of clouds,
uncoiled his coils from the Blessed One’s body, withdrew his own form, assumed the appearance of a young brahmin,
and stood before the Blessed One with palms joined in reverence, paying homage to him.
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Seclusion is bliss for one who is contented,
who has heard the Dhamma, and who sees.”
Harmlessness is happiness in the world,
restraint toward living beings;
dispassion for the world is happiness.
The transcending of sensual desires,
and the subduing of the conceit "I am"—
this indeed is the supreme happiness.
The Discourse on Mucalinda is finished.
4. The Discourse on Rājāyatana:
Then, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and [went] from the foot of the Mucalinda tree to where...
He approached the Rājāyatana tree; having approached, he sat at the foot of the Rājāyatana for seven days in a single cross-legged posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
Now at that time, the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika from Ukkala were traveling along the high road toward that region.
Then a deity who was a blood relative of the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika said this to them:
"Sirs, this Blessed One is dwelling at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree, having just attained full enlightenment;
go and honor that Blessed One with some fresh meal and a honey cake."
"That will be for your welfare and happiness for a long time.
Then the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika, taking some rice-porridge and honey-cakes, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept from us this ground meal and honey-ball, which will be for our long-term welfare and happiness.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“Tathāgatas do not accept things with their hands.”
"In what [vessel] indeed should I receive the stirred drink and the honey-ball?
Then the four Great Kings, knowing with their own minds the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One's mind, presented four stone bowls from the four directions to the Blessed One, saying:
"Here, Bhante, let the Blessed One receive the stirred drink and the honey-ball."
The Blessed One accepted the excellent meal of rice porridge and honey-cakes in his stone bowl, and having accepted them, he ate.
Then the merchants Tapussa and Bhallika, seeing that the Blessed One had finished his meal and had removed his hand from the bowl, bowed their heads at the Blessed One’s feet and said to him:
“Venerable sir, we go for refuge to the Blessed One and to the Dhamma. May the Blessed One accept us as lay followers who have gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
And they were the first lay followers in the world to take the two-fold refuge.
The Discourse on the Royal Park is finished. 5.
The Discourse on the Brahmā’s Entreaty.
Then, at the end of seven days, the Blessed One emerged from that concentration and went from the foot of the Rājāyatana tree to the Goatherd’s Banyan tree.
There, the Blessed One stayed at the foot of the Goatherd’s Banyan tree.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
“This Dhamma that I have realized is profound, hard to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.
Yet this generation delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment.
For a generation that delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment, this state—namely, specific conditionality and dependent origination—is difficult to see.
"This state too is very difficult to see: namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
If I were to teach the Dhamma, and others did not understand me, that would be weariness for me, that would be a vexation for me.
Then these verses, never heard before, occurred to the Blessed One: [The verses follow.]
“It was attained by me with difficulty;
it is now fit to be proclaimed.
[But] for those overcome by lust and hatred,”
This Dhamma is not easily awakened to;
it goes against the stream, is subtle,
profound, hard to see, and fine.
“Those who are intoxicated by passion do not see,
being shrouded by a mass of darkness.
Thus, as the Blessed One reflected, his mind inclined toward inaction, not toward teaching the Dhamma.
Then, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One’s mind, the Brahmā Sahampati thought:

"Alas, the world is perishing! Alas, the world is being destroyed! For the mind of the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, inclines toward inaction rather than toward teaching the Dhamma."
Then Brahmā Sahampati—just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—disappeared from the Brahma-world and appeared before the Blessed One.
Then Brahmā Sahampati, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One:
“May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma, may the Sugata teach the Dhamma.”
“There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, through not hearing the Dhamma, are falling away; there will be those who understand the Dhamma.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said. Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“In the past, it appeared among the Magadhans...”
The Dhamma is impure, conceived by those who are defiled;
open this door to the Deathless,
so that they may hear the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One.
Just as one standing on the peak of a mountain might see the people all around, even so,
O wise one, [behold] that which consists of the Dhamma.
Having ascended the palace, O All-Seeing One,
free from sorrow, look down upon the people overwhelmed by grief,
who are overcome by birth and old age.
Arise, O Hero, victor in battle!
O Caravan-leader, free from debt, wander through the world;
teach the Dhamma, Blessed One.
“They will come to understand.
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed Brahmā Sahampati thus:
“Brahmā, it occurred to me as well:”
“This Dhamma that I have realized is profound, hard to see, difficult to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.
Yet this generation delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment.
For a generation that delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment, this state—namely, specific conditionality and dependent origination—is difficult to see.
‘This state, too, is very difficult to see: namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
If I were to teach the Dhamma, and others did not understand me, that would be wearying for me, that would be troublesome.
And, Brahmā, these verses, never heard before, occurred to me spontaneously: [The verses follow]...’”
‘What I have attained with difficulty—
enough now to reveal it!
To those overcome by lust and hatred, [it would be hard to understand].’
This Dhamma is not easily awakened to;
it goes against the stream, is subtle,
profound, difficult to see, and minute.
“Those who are intoxicated by passion do not see,
being shrouded by a mass of darkness.
Thus, Brahmā, as I reflected, my mind inclined toward inaction rather than to teaching the Dhamma.
A second time, Brahmā Sahampati said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma; let the Sugata teach the Dhamma.
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma; there will be those who will understand the Dhamma.”
Thus spoke Brahmā Sahampati; having said this, he further said this:
"In the past, O Magadhans, there appeared a Dhamma that was impure, conceived by those still stained with defilement."
Open this door to the Deathless;
let them hear the Dhamma awakened to by the Stainless One.
Like one standing on the summit of a rocky mountain, [he surveys the world].
Just as one might look upon the multitude all around,
so too, O wise one with eyes everywhere, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, you should look out.
Free from sorrow, look upon the people overcome by sorrow,
who are oppressed by birth and old age.
Arise, O Hero, victor in battle!
“O Caravan-leader, free from debt, wander through the world;
may the Blessed One teach the Dhamma,
for there will be those who understand.”
A second time, the Blessed One said this to Brahmā Sahampati:
"Brahmā, it occurred to me too:
'This Dhamma that I have attained is profound, hard to see, hard to understand, peaceful, sublime, beyond the sphere of reasoning, subtle, and to be experienced by the wise.'"
But this generation delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, rejoices in attachment.
For a generation that delights in attachment, takes delight in attachment, and rejoices in attachment, this point is difficult to see: namely, specific conditionality and dependent origination.
And this point is even more difficult to see: namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
‘If I were to teach the Dhamma, and others did not understand me, that would be weariness to me, that would be vexation to me.
And then, Brahmā, these marvelous verses, never heard before, occurred to me:
‘With difficulty have I attained it;’
Enough now with further exposition;
this Dhamma is not easily awakened to by those overcome by lust and hatred.
Those who are stained by passion will not see that which goes against the stream, which is subtle, profound, difficult to see, and minute.
“Enveloped by the mass of darkness.
Thus, Brahmā, as I reflected, my mind inclined toward inaction, not toward teaching the Dhamma.
A third time, Brahmā Sahampati said this to the Blessed One:
“Teach the Dhamma, Bhante! Let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma!
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma; there will be those who will understand the Dhamma.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said. Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“In the past, O Magadhans,
there appeared a Dhamma that was impure, conceived by those still stained with defilements.
Open this door to the Deathless!
Listen to the Dhamma realized by the Stainless One.
Just as one standing on the summit of a rocky mountain might see the people all around, so too [does he see].
Having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, which is like that, O wise one,
with eyes seeing all around,
you, free from sorrow, look upon the people overwhelmed by grief.
Behold those overcome by birth and old age!
Arise, O Hero, victor in battle!
O Caravan-leader, free from debt, wander through the world.
“Teach the Dhamma, Blessed One;
there will be those who understand.
Then the Blessed One, having understood the Brahmā’s request and out of compassion for beings, surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha.
As the Blessed One surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha, he saw beings with little dust on their eyes and with much dust on their eyes,
with keen faculties and with dull faculties, of good disposition and of bad disposition, easy to instruct and difficult to instruct;
some dwelling perceiving the fear of blame regarding the next world, and others dwelling not perceiving the fear of blame regarding the next world.
Just as in a pond of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses— some of those blue, pink,
or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not rise above the water,
and thrive submerged within it; while some of those blue, pink, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water...
They grew and remained submerged in water; some lotuses—blue, red, or white—born in the water and grown in the water, stood rising above the water, unsullied by the water.
In the same way, as the Blessed One surveyed the world with the eye of a Buddha, he saw beings with little dust on their eyes and those with much dust on their eyes.
Seeing some with keen faculties and some with dull faculties, some of good disposition and some of bad disposition, some easy to instruct and some difficult to instruct,
some dwelling perceiving the fear of blame and the world beyond, and some dwelling not perceiving the fear of blame and the world beyond,
Brahmā Sahampati addressed him in verse:
“The doors to the Deathless are opened for those who have ears;
let them release their faith.
Perceiving harm in it, I did not speak what is wholesome.”
“O Brahmā, the sublime Dhamma among humans!
Then Brahmā Sahampati, thinking,
“I have been granted permission by the Blessed One to teach the Dhamma,” paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
The Discourse on the Request of Brahmā is finished.
6. The Discourse on the Group of Five.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
“To whom, indeed, should I first teach the Dhamma?
Who will understand this Dhamma most quickly?
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“This Āḷāra Kālāma is wise, competent, and intelligent; he has long been one whose nature is free from much dust.
Suppose I were to teach this Dhamma first to Āḷāra Kālāma; he would quickly understand this Dhamma.
Then a hidden deity informed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago.”
The knowledge also arose in the Blessed One: “Āḷāra Kālāma died seven days ago.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“Āḷāra Kālāma was indeed a man of great loss.”
"For if he were to hear this Dhamma, he would quickly understand it.
Then the Blessed One thought:
"To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?"
“Who will quickly understand this Dhamma?
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“This Udaka Rāmaputta is wise, competent, and intelligent; for a long time he has been one whose nature is free from much defilement.”
"What if I were to teach the Dhamma first to Udaka Rāmaputta? He would quickly understand this Dhamma.
Then an invisible deity informed the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, Udaka Rāmaputta died last night.
And knowledge arose in the Blessed One as well: "Udaka Rāmaputta died last night."
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“Udaka Rāmaputta is a man of great wisdom;
if he were to hear this Dhamma, he would quickly understand it.”
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?
Who will understand this Dhamma most quickly?”
Then the Blessed One thought:
“The group-of-five monks have been very helpful to me, for they attended upon me when I was intent on striving;
what if I were to teach the Dhamma first to the group-of-five monks?”
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
"Where are the group-of-five bhikkhus dwelling now?
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Blessed One saw the group-of-five bhikkhus dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.
Then the Blessed One, having dwelt at Uruvelā for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Bārāṇasī.
Along the way between Gayā and the Bodhi tree, the Ājīvaka Upaka saw the Blessed One traveling on the highway; seeing him, he said this to the Blessed One:
“Friend, your faculties are serene, and the color of your skin is pure and bright.”
"Friend, for whose sake have you gone forth?
Who is your teacher?
Or whose Dhamma do you approve?"
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed the Ājīvaka Upaka with verses:
“I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all;
I am unsullied by any phenomena.”
Having abandoned everything and being liberated through the destruction of craving,
having realized this for myself through direct knowledge, whom should I point to as my teacher? I have no teacher.
No one equal to me is found;
in this world with its devas,
there is no rival to me.
For I am the Worthy One in the world;
I am the unsurpassed Teacher;
I alone am the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
I have become cool and attained Nibbāna.
To set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma,
I shall go to the city of Kāsī.
“In a world that has become blind,
I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.
“Friend, as you claim for yourself, you are indeed an Arahant, a Conqueror of the Infinite.”
“Indeed, those like me are victors,
who have attained the destruction of the taints;
evil states have been conquered by me.”
"Therefore, Upaka, I am the Conqueror.
When this was said, the Ājīvaka Upaka replied, "Perhaps so, friend," and shaking his head, he took a byway and departed.
Then the Blessed One, wandering by stages on his journey, approached Bārāṇasī, the Deer Park at Isipatana, where the group of five monks were staying.
The group-of-five monks saw the Blessed One coming from afar;
having seen him, they made an agreement among themselves:
"Friends, here comes the ascetic Gotama, one who has become luxurious, who has fallen away from his striving and has reverted to luxury."
"Therefore, he is neither to be saluted nor to be risen for; nor is his bowl and robe to be received.
Rather, a seat should be set out, and if he so desires, he shall sit.
However, as the Blessed One approached the group of five monks, the group of five monks were unable to maintain their agreement.

Without hesitating, they went out to meet the Blessed One; one received his bowl and robe, one prepared a seat, one set out water for washing the feet, one a footstool, and one placed a foot-washing stone.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat, and having sat down, he washed his feet.
They addressed the Blessed One by name and with the familiar term "friend.
When this was said, the Blessed One said to the group of five monks:
"Monks, do not address the Tathāgata by name and with the familiar term 'friend'."
“Monks, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened one. Give ear, monks; the Deathless has been attained. I instruct you; I teach you the Dhamma.
Practicing in accordance with my instructions, before long you will realize that supreme goal for which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
“...and you shall dwell having realized for yourselves, through direct knowledge, and having attained in this very life, the consummation of the holy life.
When this was said, the group of five monks said this to the Blessed One:
“Friend Gotama, by that conduct, by that practice, and by that performance of austerities, you did not even attain [superhuman states].”
“Since you are now one who indulges in abundance, who has abandoned striving and turned back toward abundance, how will you attain any superhuman state, any distinction in noble knowledge and vision?
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus of the group of five as follows:
“Monks, the Tathāgata does not indulge in abundance, nor is he one who has strayed from exertion, nor has he turned back toward abundance.
Monks, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha.
Give ear, monks; the Deathless has been attained. I instruct you; I teach the Dhamma.”
"Practicing in accordance with what has been instructed, before long you will,

by realizing it for yourselves through direct knowledge, enter and dwell in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, even in this very life."
A second time, the bhikkhus of the group of five said this to the Blessed One...
[as before] ...A second time, the Blessed One said this to the bhikkhus of the group of five...
[as before] ...A third time, the bhikkhus of the group of five said this to the Blessed One:
“Friend Gotama, even by that conduct, by that practice, and by those austerities,

you did not attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones; how then, now that you are luxurious, have abandoned your striving, and have turned back to luxury, will you attain any superhuman state, any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones?”
When this was said, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus of the group of five:
“Bhikkhus, do you recognize that such a thing has been proclaimed by me before this?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened one. Give ear, bhikkhus; I shall instruct you in that which has been attained—the Deathless. I teach the Dhamma.

Practicing in accordance with what has been instructed, before long you yourselves will realize that supreme goal for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.”
“Having realized for yourselves through direct knowledge in this very life the culmination of the holy life, you shall abide having attained it.
The Blessed One was able to convince the group of five monks.
Then the group of five monks listened to the Blessed One; they lent an ear and applied their minds to understand.
Then the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
“Monks, these two extremes should not be pursued by one who has gone forth.
Which two?
“Monks, this devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires—which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial—and this devotion to self-mortification—which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial:

having avoided both these extremes, monks, the Middle Way has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; it produces vision, it produces knowledge, and it leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to self-awakening, and to Nibbāna.”
And what, monks, is that middle way realized by the Tathāgata, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna?
It is this very Noble Eightfold Path; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
"This, monks, is that Middle Way realized by the Tathāgata, which produces vision, produces knowledge, and leads to peace, direct knowledge, full enlightenment, and Nibbāna.
And this, monks, is the Noble Truth of Suffering:

birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, and not to obtain what one desires is also suffering."
In brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
And this, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering:
it is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; that is to say:—
Craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Now, monks, this is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering:
it is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, its abandonment, its release, and its non-attachment.
And this, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering—the Noble Eightfold Path itself; that is to say:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
“‘This is the noble truth of suffering’—thus, monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
‘That this noble truth of suffering must be fully understood’—thus, monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.”
“Monks, regarding this noble truth of suffering as something to be fully understood: in regard to things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
Regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering: in regard to things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.”

“Monks, regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering as something to be abandoned: in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
Regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering as having been abandoned: in regard to things unheard before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.”
“‘This is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering’—thus, monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true insight, and light.
‘And this noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized’—thus, monks, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye, knowledge, wisdom, true insight, and light.”

"Furthermore, monks, regarding this noble truth of the cessation of suffering as having been realized: in regard to things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
Regarding this noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: in regard to things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light."
"Furthermore, monks, regarding this noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as something to be developed:
vision arose in me concerning these things unheard of before; knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge arose, and light arose."
"Furthermore, monks, regarding this noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering as having been developed:

And a measureless, sublime radiance appeared in the world, surpassing the splendor of the devas.

“Koṇḍañña has indeed understood! Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!”

That itself was the full ordination of those venerable ones.
Then the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks:
“Form, monks, is non-self.
For if this form, monks, were self, this form would not lead to affliction, and it would be possible regarding form—”
‘May my form be thus; may my form not be thus.
But because form is non-self, monks, therefore form leads to affliction, and one cannot obtain regarding form:
‘May my form be thus; may my form not be thus.’
Feeling is not-self.

But because feeling, monks, is not-self, therefore feeling leads to affliction, and it is not possible regarding feeling [to say]:
"Let my feeling be thus; let my feeling not be thus.

"Let my perception be thus; let my perception not be thus.

‘May my volitional formations be thus; may my volitional formations not be thus.’
Consciousness is not-self.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.

This is how it should be seen with correct wisdom as it really is.

Now at that time in Bārāṇasī there was a young man of good family named Yasa, the son of a wealthy merchant, who was very delicate.
He had three palaces:

Then, having woken up beforehand, the young man Yasa saw his own retinue sleeping:

Upon seeing this, the danger became manifest to him, and his mind settled into disenchantment.
Then the young man Yasa uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Alas, we are beset! Alas, we are overwhelmed!
Then the young man Yasa, having put on his golden sandals, went toward the door of his residence.

The account of the going forth of the four lay companions is concluded.

Thus ends the account of the going forth of the fifty friends who were householders.
8. The Discourse on Māra.
Then the Blessed One addressed those bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, I am freed from all snares, both those that are divine and those that are human.”
You too, monks, are freed from all snares—both those of the devas and those of humans.
Wander, monks, on tour for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans.
Let not two of you go by the same way.
"Proclaim, monks, the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing; reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
There are beings with little dust in their eyes who are perishing through not hearing the Dhamma; there will be those who understand the Dhamma.
And I too, monks, shall go to Uruvelā, to the village of Senāni, for the purpose of teaching the Dhamma."
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“You are bound by all snares, both those that are divine and those that are human.”
"You are bound by great fetters;
you shall not escape me, ascetic!
"I am released from all snares."
Whether divine or human,
I am liberated from the great bond;
you, O End-maker, are slain.
“The snare that moves through the air,
which wanders in the mind—
with that I shall afflict you.”
“O ascetic, you shall not escape from me!
“Forms, sounds, tastes, smells,
and delightful tangibles— ”
"Here my desire has vanished;

Then Māra the Evil One—

9. The Discourse on Going-forth and Ordination.

Now at that time, monks were bringing those seeking the going-forth and those seeking full ordination from various directions and various countries, thinking, "The Blessed One will give them the going-forth; he will give them the full ordination.
There, both the monks and those seeking the going-forth and those seeking full ordination became exhausted.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:
"At present, monks from various directions and various countries bring those seeking the going-forth and seeking the full ordination, thinking:

There, both the monks grew weary, as did those seeking the going-forth and those seeking full ordination. [The Blessed One thought:
"What if I were to authorize the monks:
'Now, monks, you yourselves should grant the going-forth and the full ordination in those various directions and in those various regions'?"
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and, having given a discourse on the Dhamma concerning this cause and this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“In this regard, bhikkhus, while I was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in my mind:
‘At present, bhikkhus, monks bring from various directions and various countries those who desire the going forth and those who desire full ordination.’”
‘The Blessed One will grant the going-forth and the full ordination,’ thinking thus, the monks here grew weary, as did those seeking the going-forth and those seeking the full ordination.
“What if I were to authorize the monks themselves: ‘Now, monks, you yourselves should grant the going-forth and the full ordination in those various directions and in those various regions’?
“I authorize it, monks; now you yourselves should grant the going-forth and the full ordination in those various directions.”
In those directions and in those various countries, you should grant the going-forth and the full ordination.
And furthermore, monks, one should be granted the going-forth and the full ordination in this way:
first, having had the hair and beard shaved off, having had him clothed in saffron-colored robes, and having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder...
Having had [him] have the monks’ feet worshipped, having had him sit in the kneeling posture, and having had him raise his joined palms, he should be told: “Speak thus:
‘I go for refuge to the Buddha;’”
I go for refuge to the Dhamma;
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
A second time, I go for refuge to the Buddha.
For a second time, I go for refuge to the Dhamma;
for a second time, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
For a third time, I go for refuge to the Buddha.
“‘For a third time, I go for refuge to the Dhamma;
for a third time, I go for refuge to the Saṅgha.
Monks, I allow you to grant the going forth and the full ordination by means of these three goings for refuge.”
The discourse on full ordination by means of the threefold going for refuge is finished.
10. The Second Discourse on Māra.
Then the Blessed One, having completed the rains retreat, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, through wise attention and wise right effort, I have attained supreme liberation; I have realized supreme liberation.
You too, monks, through wise attention and wise right effort, attain supreme liberation; realize supreme liberation.
Then Māra the Evil One approached the Blessed One, and having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:

both those that are divine and those that are human;
you are bound by the great fetters.”
“O ascetic, you shall not escape from me!
[The Buddha replied: “I am released from the snares of Māra, both those that are divine and those that are human.”
“I am liberated from the great bond;
you are defeated, O Ender!
Then Māra the Evil One—
“The Blessed One knows me; the Sugata knows me,” he said, and pained and dejected, he vanished right there.
The Second Discourse on Māra is finished.
11. The Story of the Group of Bhaddas.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Bārāṇasī for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Uruvelā.
Then the Blessed One, descending from the road, approached a certain grove; having approached it and entered deep into that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree.
Now at that time, about thirty friends of the Bhaddavaggiya group, together with their wives, were sporting in that grove.
One had no wife;
for his sake, a courtesan had been brought.
Then, while they were sporting heedlessly, that courtesan took their goods and fled.
Then those companions, while performing services for their friend and searching for that woman, wandered through that grove and saw the Blessed One sitting at the foot of a certain tree.
Having seen him, they approached the Blessed One and said to him:
"Venerable sir, has the Blessed One perhaps seen a certain woman?"
“But what, young men, do you want with a woman?
“Here, venerable sir, we thirty friends from the Bhaddavaggiya group, together with our wives, have been enjoying ourselves in this forest grove.
One of us had no wife.”
"For his sake, a courtesan was brought here.
Then, venerable sir, while we were negligent and enjoying ourselves with her, that courtesan took our goods and fled.
We, venerable sir, being companions who perform services for one another, have been wandering through this forest grove searching for that woman."
“What do you think, princes? Which would be better for you:
that you should seek out a woman, or that you should seek out yourselves?
“Venerable sir, this alone would be better for us: that we should seek out ourselves.”
“In that case, young men, sit down; I shall teach you the Dhamma.
“Very well, venerable sir,” those friends of the Bhaddavaggiya group replied, and having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
To them the Blessed One delivered a graduated discourse, namely:
He proclaimed a discourse on giving, a discourse on virtue, a discourse on heaven; he revealed the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.

When the Blessed One knew that their minds were ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, then he revealed that which is the special Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would properly take the dye;
In that very moment, on that very seat, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in them:
"Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation.

Having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma; having crossed over doubt, being free from perplexity, having gained self-confidence, and becoming independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, they said this to the Blessed One:

“Come, monks,” the Blessed One said, “the Dhamma is well-expounded;
live the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.”
That was the full ordination of those venerable ones.
The account of the companions of the Bhaddavaggiya group is finished.
The second recitation section.
12. The Discourse on the Miracle at Uruvelā Then the Blessed One, traveling by stages on his journey, arrived at Uruvelā.
Now at that time, three matted-hair ascetics were residing in Uruvelā: Uruvelakassapa, Nadīkassapa, and Gayākassapa.
They were Uruvelakassapa, Nadīkassapa, and Gayākassapa.
Among them, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa was the leader, guide, chief, foremost, and preeminent of five hundred matted-hair ascetics.
The matted-hair ascetic Nadīkassapa was the leader, guide, chief, foremost, and preeminent of three hundred matted-hair ascetics.
The matted-hair ascetic Gayākassapa was the leader, guide, chief, foremost, and preeminent of two hundred matted-hair ascetics.
Then the Blessed One approached the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa; having approached, he said this to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
"If it is not troublesome for you, Kassapa, we would stay for one night in the fire-hall."
“It is not troublesome for me, Great Ascetic, but there is a fierce Naga king here, powerful and venomous, with terrible poison; let him not harm you.
A second time, the Blessed One said this to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
“If it is not troublesome for you, Kassapa, would we stay for one night in the fire-hall?”
“It is not troublesome for me, Great Ascetic; however, there is a fierce Nāga king here, powerful and venomous, with terrible poison. Do not let him harm you.
A third time, the Blessed One said this to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
“If it is not troublesome for you, Kassapa, would we stay for one night in the fire-hall?”
“It is not that I am reluctant, Great Ascetic; however, there is here a fierce Naga king, a powerful and venomous serpent of terrible poison. Do not let him harm you.
“Even if he should not harm me, come now, Kassapa, please grant me the use of the fire-hall.
“Dwell as you please, Great Ascetic.”
Then the Blessed One, having entered the kitchen, prepared a grass mat and sat down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
That nāga saw that the Blessed One had entered; seeing him, he became dejected and emitted smoke.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“What if I were to overcome this nāga’s fire with my own fire, without destroying his skin, hide, flesh, sinews, bones, or marrow?
Then the Blessed One performed such a feat of psychic power that he emitted smoke.
Thereupon, unable to endure the insult, the nāga burst into flames.
The Blessed One, too, having entered the fire-element, blazed up.
Both of them being ablaze, the fire-hall became as if on fire, fully aflame, and glowing.
Then those matted-hair ascetics, having surrounded the fire-hall, spoke thus:
“Ah, how handsome indeed is that great ascetic, yet he is being tormented by the nāga!
Then, at the end of that night, the Blessed One— without harming the nāga’s skin, hide, flesh, sinews, bones, or marrow—
overpowered its fire with his own fire, placed it in his alms bowl, and [departed].
He showed him to Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic, saying:
"Kassapa, this Nāga has been subdued by you; let fire meet fire.
Then it occurred to Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic:

“The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that he will, by means of his own fiery energy, consume the fiery energy of the fierce Naga King, the possessor of psychic power, the venomous snake of terrible poison; yet he is certainly not an Arahant like I am.
Thus the Blessed One spoke to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa on the banks of the Nerañjarā River.
“If it is not troublesome for you, Kassapa,
let us stay tonight in the fire-hall.
“It is not troublesome for me, Great Ascetic.”
It is out of a desire for my own welfare that I restrain you;
for here dwells a fierce Naga king,
possessed of psychic power, a venomous serpent of terrible bite.
“Therefore, do not harm him.
“Even if he would not harm me,
come now, Kassapa, please grant me permission to use the fire-hall.”
Knowing that it was being given,
he entered without fear, having transcended all dread.
Seeing the seer who had entered,
The serpent-king, dejected, sent forth smoke;
but the human-nāga, with a joyful mind and exalted heart,
sent forth smoke there as well.
Unable to endure that insult,
the Naga King blazed up like a fire;
he was highly skilled in the fire-element.
The human nāga also blazed there.
When both were set ablaze,
the fire-chamber was burning, blazing, and set aflame.
The matted-hair ascetics cried out,
"Oh, how handsome is this great ascetic!
He is being harassed by a nāga," they said.
Then, with the passing of that night,
the flames of the nāga were extinguished,
but those of the possessor of psychic power remained.
The flames are of many colors:
blue, then red, madder-red,
yellow, and the color of crystal.
In the body of Aṅgīrasa,
flames of many colors arise;
having placed them within his bowl, [he emits them].
He showed a live snake to the brahmin, saying:
"Kassapa, here is a snake for you;
let fire consume its fire."
Then the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, having gained deep confidence in the Blessed One through this miracle of psychic power, said to the Blessed One:
"Stay right here, Great Ascetic; I shall provide you with regular meals.
This was the first miracle.
Then the Blessed One dwelt in a certain grove not far from the hermitage of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa.
Then, when the night had advanced, the Four Great Kings, having illuminated that entire grove with their surpassing beauty, approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, [they stood] in the four directions.
They stood there like great masses of fire.
Then, at the end of that night, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready."
“Who were they, Great Ascetic, who at the end of the night, with such surpassing beauty,
having illuminated the entire grove, approached you, and having approached and paid homage to you, stood in the four directions like great masses of fire?”
“Kassapa, these four Great Kings have come to me to hear the Dhamma.
Then it occurred to the yogi Uruvelakassapa:
“Powerful indeed is this Great Ascetic, possessed of great majesty, since even the four Great Kings have come to him to hear the Dhamma; yet he is not an Arahant like I am.”
Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, stayed in that very grove of trees.
This was the second miracle.
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, at the end of the night, with surpassing beauty, [illuminated] the entire grove of trees.

Having illuminated [the area], he approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side like a great mass of fire, even more brilliant and exquisite than his previous splendor.
Then, at the end of that night, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
“It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready.

Who was that, Great Ascetic, who at the end of the night, with a most excellent complexion, having illuminated the entire grove, approached you, and having approached and paid homage to you, stood to one side?”
“Is it like a great mass of fire, more brilliant and more sublime than all previous splendors?
“That was Sakka, lord of the devas, Kassapa, who approached me to hear the Dhamma.
Then this occurred to Uruvelakassapa, the yogi:
“The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, since even Sakka, the lord of the devas, will approach him to listen to the Dhamma; yet he is not an Arahant like I am.
Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, dwelt in that very grove.
This was the third miracle.
Then, when the night had advanced, Brahmā Sahampati, with a magnificent radiance,
illuminating the entire grove, approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One,
he stood to one side like a great mass of fire, surpassing and excelling the previous splendors of color and appearance.
Then, at the end of that night, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready.
Who was it, Great Ascetic, who during the night, with such surpassing beauty, illuminated the entire grove?"

“Having illumined it, he approached you; having approached and paid homage to you, he stood to one side like a great mass of fire, surpassing and excelling the previous splendors in color and radiance?
“That, Kassapa, was Brahmā Sahampati who approached me to hear the Dhamma.”
Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
"The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, since even Brahmā Sahampati will approach him to hear the Dhamma; yet he is not an Arahant as I am.
Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, stayed in that very grove.
This was the fourth miracle.

Now at that time, a great sacrifice had been prepared for the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, and the entire regions of Aṅga and Magadha were desirous of coming forth, bringing with them abundant food, both hard and soft.
Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
“Now a great sacrifice has been prepared for me, and people from the whole of Aṅga and Magadha will come bringing abundant hard food and soft food.
If the Great Ascetic performs a miracle before this great multitude, the gain and honor of the Great Ascetic will increase, while my own gain and honor will diminish.
Oh, it would be well if the Great Ascetic did not come tomorrow!”

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, went to Uttarakuru; having brought almsfood from there and eaten it at Lake Anotatta, he spent the day’s abiding right there.
Then, at the end of that night, the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa approached the Blessed One and, having approached, said this to the Blessed One:
“It is time, Great Ascetic; the meal is ready.”
"Why, Great Ascetic, did you not come yesterday?
Yet we were mindful of you,

“A portion of solid food and soft food has been set aside for you.
“Did it not occur to you, Kassapa:
‘Now a great sacrifice is being prepared for me, and throughout the whole of Aṅga and Magadha there is abundant solid food’?”

‘Taking their food, they will go forth; if the Great Ascetic performs a feat of psychic power before the great multitude, the gain and honor of the Great Ascetic will increase, while my own gain and honor will diminish.
Oh, would that the Great Ascetic did not come tomorrow!’”
“Then, Kassapa, having understood the reflection in your mind with my own mind, I went to Uttarakuru, brought back almsfood from there, ate it at Lake Anotatta, and spent the day’s rest right there.
Then this occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
“The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that he can understand even the mind with his own mind; yet he is not an Arahant like me.”
Then the Blessed One, having eaten the meal of the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa, dwelt in that very grove.
This was the fifth miracle.
Now at that time, a rag-robe had come into the possession of the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“Where now might I wash this rag-robe?

“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One wash this rag-robe here.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“On what now shall I rub this rag-robe?”
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One’s mind, set down a large stone, saying:
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One rub the rag-robe here.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
“What indeed can I grasp to pull myself up?
Then a deity dwelling in a *kakudha* tree, knowing with her own mind the reflection in the Blessed One’s mind, bent down a branch:
“Here, Bhante, let the Blessed One grasp this and pull himself up.”
Then the Blessed One thought:
"Upon what now should I cast this rag-robe?
Then Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One's mind, set down a great rock.
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One cast aside his rag-robe here.

"Why is it, Great Ascetic, that this lotus pond was not here before, yet now this lotus pond is here?
These stones were not placed here before;
by whom have these stones been placed here?"
“Previously this branch of the *kakudha* tree was not bent down; it is this very branch that is bent down now.
“Kassapa, here a rag-robe arose for me.
Then, Kassapa, this thought occurred to me:”
‘Where indeed might I wash this rag-robe?
Then, Kassapa, Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in my mind, dug a lotus pond with his hand and said to me:
‘Here, Bhante, let the Blessed One wash the rag-robe.’”
In the evening, Kassapa, a lotus pond was dug by a non-human being with its hand.
Then, Kassapa, this thought occurred to me:
“On what indeed shall I beat out my rag-robe?”
Then, Kassapa, Sakka, lord of the devas, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in my mind, set down a great rock, saying:
"Venerable sir, let the Blessed One rub the rag-robe here.
This, Kassapa, was the rock set down by a non-human being.
Then, Kassapa, this occurred to me:
"What indeed can I grasp to pull myself up?

“This stone, Kassapa, was set down by a non-human being this evening.
Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
“The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, since even Sakka, lord of the devas, performs service for him; yet he is not an arahant like me.”

“Here, Kassapa, having dismissed you, I took a fruit from the rose-apple tree after which ‘Jambudīpa’ is named; having arrived first, I am sitting in the fire-hall.
This, Kassapa, is the rose-apple fruit, endowed with excellence of color, excellence of fragrance, and excellence of flavor.”
“If you wish, enjoy it.

Then this thought occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:

he has taken a fruit from the rose-apple tree after which ‘Jambudīpa’ is named, and having returned first, is sitting in the fire-hall;

“Let it be split, Great Ascetic.”

Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
"The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that even pieces of wood split apart; yet he is certainly not an Arahant like I am."
Now at that time, those matted-hair ascetics, wishing to tend the sacrificial fire, were unable to kindle it.
Then it occurred to those matted-hair ascetics:
"Without a doubt, this is due to the supernatural power of the Great Ascetic, since we are unable to kindle the fire."
Then the Blessed One said this to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
“Kassapa, let the fires be kindled.
“Let them be kindled, Great Ascetic,” he replied.
At once, five hundred fires blazed up.
Then it occurred to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:
"The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that even fires can be ignited by him; yet he is not an Arahant like I am."
Now at that time, those matted-hair ascetics, having tended the fire, were unable to extinguish it.
Then it occurred to those matted-hair ascetics:
"Without a doubt, this is the power of the psychic majesty of the Great Ascetic, such that we are unable to extinguish the fire."
Then the Blessed One said this to the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa:

“Let them be extinguished, Great Ascetic.”

Now at that time, during the cold winter nights in the intervals between the eighth days, at the season of snowfall, those matted-hair ascetics were emerging from, submerging in, and repeatedly performing the act of emerging and submerging in the river Nerañjarā.

Now at that time, a great unseasonable storm-cloud rained down, and a great flood arose.

Then this thought occurred to the Blessed One:
“What if I were to drive back the water on all sides and walk up and down in the middle on ground covered with dust?

Then the matted-hair ascetic Uruvelakassapa—

“The Great Ascetic is indeed of great psychic power and great majesty, in that he can even cause the water not to flow; yet he is certainly not an Arahant as I am.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:

Then the Blessed One said this to Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic:

Nor do you possess that practice by which you might become an arahant or enter the path to arahantship.
Then Uruvelakassapa the matted-hair ascetic prostrated himself at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One:

“Kassapa, you are the leader, guide, foremost, chief, and head of five hundred matted-hair ascetics.
First, seek their permission; they will do as they think fit.”
Then the yogi Uruvelakassapa went to those yogis and, having approached them, said this to them:
“Sirs, I wish to lead the holy life under the Great Ascetic; do as you think best.
“For a long time, sir, we have had great confidence in the Great Ascetic. If you, sir, will lead the holy life under the Great Ascetic, then we all shall lead the holy life under the Great Ascetic.”
Then those hair-matted ascetics, having cast their hair, their matted locks, their carrying-poles, and their fire-offerings into the water, approached the Blessed One.

“Venerable sir, may we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive the full admission.”
“Come, monks,” the Blessed One said, “the Dhamma is well-expounded;
lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
That was the full ordination of those venerable ones.
The matted-hair ascetic Nadīkassapa saw the hair, the matted locks, the carrying-pole, and the fire-offerings being carried away by the water; having seen this, it occurred to him:

He sent word to the matted-hair ascetics:
“Go and find out about my brother.
Then he, together with three hundred matted-hair ascetics, approached the Venerable Uruvelakassapa; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Uruvelakassapa:
“Is this, Kassapa, indeed better?”
“Yes, friends, this is better.
Then those matted-hair ascetics, having cast their hair, their matted locks, their carrying-poles, and their fire-offerings into the water, approached the Blessed One.

lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.”
That was the full ordination of those venerable ones.
Then the matted-hair ascetic Gayākassapa saw the hair, the matted locks, the carrying-pole, and the fire-offerings being carried away by the water; seeing this, it occurred to him:
"May no harm have come to my brothers!"
He sent for the matted-hair ascetics, saying, "Go and find my brothers.
Then Sāma, together with two hundred matted-hair ascetics, approached the Venerable Uruvelakassapa; having approached, he said this to the Venerable Uruvelakassapa:
“Is this, Kassapa, indeed better?

Then those matted-hair ascetics cast their hair, their matted locks, their carrying-poles, their fire-sacrifices, and their ritual implements into the water.
They approached the Blessed One; having approached, they prostrated with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and said this to him:
“Venerable sir, may we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive the full admission.
“Come, monks,” the Blessed One said.
“The Dhamma is well-expounded; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
That itself was their full ordination.
By the Blessed One’s resolve, five hundred pieces of wood did not split, yet they split.
The fires did not blaze up, yet they blazed up;
they were not extinguished, yet they were extinguished;
he manifested five hundred pots with spouts.
By this method, there were three thousand five hundred miracles.
Then the Blessed One, having dwelt at Uruvelā for as long as he pleased, set out for Gayāsīsa together with a great Saṅgha of monks—a thousand monks, all of whom had formerly been jaṭilas.
There, indeed, the Blessed One dwelt at Gayā on Gayāsīsa together with that thousand of monks.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, everything is burning.
And what, bhikkhus, is that everything which is burning?”
The eye is aflame; forms are aflame; eye-consciousness is aflame; eye-contact is aflame;
and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is aflame.
By what is it aflame?
It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; I say it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

The ear is ablaze, sounds are ablaze, ear-consciousness is ablaze, ear-contact is ablaze, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by ear-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is ablaze.
Ablaze with what?
I say it is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

The nose is ablaze, odors are ablaze, nose-consciousness is ablaze, nose-contact is ablaze, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by nose-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is ablaze.

It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; I say it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

By what is it ablaze?
It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; I say it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

The body is ablaze, tangibles are ablaze, body-consciousness is ablaze, body-contact is ablaze, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by body-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is ablaze.
By what is it ablaze?
It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; I say it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.

The mind is ablaze, mental phenomena are ablaze, mind-consciousness is ablaze, and mind-contact is ablaze. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is ablaze.
By what is it ablaze?
It is ablaze with the fire of lust, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion; I say it is ablaze with birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye and becomes disenchanted with forms.
One becomes disenchanted with eye-consciousness; one becomes disenchanted with eye-contact;
and one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
One becomes disenchanted with the ear; one becomes disenchanted with sounds … [and so on] …
One becomes disenchanted with the nose and disenchanted with odors... [and so on] ...
one becomes disenchanted with the tongue and disenchanted with tastes... [and so on] ...
one becomes disenchanted with the body and disenchanted with tangibles... [and so on].
One becomes disenchanted with the mind, one becomes disenchanted with mental phenomena, one becomes disenchanted with mind-consciousness,
one becomes disenchanted with mind-contact; and one becomes disenchanted with whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact— whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
“Through disenchantment, one becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, one is liberated. In liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands:
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And while this exposition was being spoken, the minds of those one thousand monks were liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
The Discourse on the Simile of the Burning House is finished.
The Third Recitation Section, concerning the Miracle at Uruvelā, is finished.
13. The Account of the Meeting with Bimbisāra.

Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Gayāsīsa for as long as he pleased, set out on a walking tour toward Rājagaha together with a great community of monks—a thousand monks, all of whom were formerly jaṭila ascetics.
As the Blessed One proceeded by stages on his walking tour, he arrived at Rājagaha.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Rājagaha in the Laṭṭhivana, at the Suppatiṭṭha Shrine.
King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha heard:
"The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakya clan, has arrived at Rājagaha and is staying at Rājagaha in the Laṭṭhivana, at the Suppatiṭṭha Shrine.
A fine report concerning the excellence of that Blessed One Gotama has spread abroad thus:"

"Such indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans, by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure."
“It is indeed good to see such Arahants.

Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, surrounded by twelve myriads of brahmin householders of Magadha, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Those twelve myriads of brahmin householders of Magadha also—some of them, having paid homage to the Blessed One...
Some sat down to one side; some exchanged greetings with the Blessed One and, having concluded the polite and courteous conversation, sat down to one side;
some extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One and sat down to one side;
some announced their name and clan in the presence of the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Some sat down to one side in silence.
Then it occurred to those twelve myriads of Magadhan brahmins and householders:
"Does the Great Ascetic lead the holy life under Uruvelā Kassapa, or does Uruvelā Kassapa lead the holy life under the Great Ascetic?"

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the minds of those twelve myriads of Magadhan brahmins and householders, addressed the Venerable Uruvelakassapa in verse:
"What did you see, O dweller of Uruvelā, that you,
though emaciated in appearance, abandoned the fire-sacrifice?"
“I ask you this matter, Kassapa:
How have you abandoned the fire-sacrifice?
“In forms, sounds, and likewise tastes...”
And women desire sacrifices;
knowing that this is a stain among acquisitions,
one does not delight in what is sacrificed or offered.
“Right here your mind found no delight,
Kassapa,” said the Blessed One,
“in forms, sounds, and likewise in tastes.”
"Now, who indeed in the world of gods and humans is delighted in mind? Tell me this, Kassapa.
"Having seen the state of peace, free from acquisitions—"
One who possesses nothing, unattached to the realm of sense-desires,
who does not become otherwise, and is not led by others—
therefore, such a one does not delight in sacrifice or offering.
Then the Venerable Uruvelakassapa rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and said this to the Blessed One:
“The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am a disciple.
The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am a disciple.”
Then it occurred to those twelve myriads of Magadhan brahmins and householders:
"Uruvelakassapa is living the holy life under the Great Ascetic.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the minds of those twelve myriads of Magadhan brahmins and householders, gave them a progressive discourse, namely:
He proclaimed a discourse on giving, a discourse on virtue, and a discourse on heaven; he explained the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit of renunciation.
When the Blessed One knew that their minds were ready, pliable, free from hindrances, uplifted, and confident, he then set forth the Dhamma teaching peculiar to Buddhas:
suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Just as a clean cloth, free from dark stains, would perfectly absorb a dye, even so,
for eleven myriads of Magadhan brahmins and householders headed by Bimbisāra, right there on their seats, the dustless, stainless Dhamma-eye arose:
"Whatever is subject to origination is all subject to cessation."
He declared himself a lay follower for as long as life shall last.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, known the Dhamma, and plunged into the Dhamma;
having crossed over doubt and being free from perplexity, having attained fearlessness and become independent of others in the Teacher’s instruction, addressed the Blessed One thus:
“Venerable sir, formerly when I was a prince, I had five hopes, all of which have now been fulfilled for me.
Venerable sir, formerly when I was a prince, it occurred to me:
‘Oh, that they might anoint me as king! This, venerable sir, was my first hope; it has now been fulfilled for me.”
‘And may a Worthy One, a Perfectly Enlightened One, enter my realm’—this, venerable sir, was my second consolation, and it has now been fulfilled for me.
‘And may I attend upon that Blessed One’—this, venerable sir, was my third consolation, and it has now been fulfilled for me.
‘And may that Blessed One teach me the Dhamma’—this, venerable sir, was my fourth consolation, and it has now been fulfilled for me.
‘May I understand the Dhamma of that Blessed One’—this, venerable sir, was my fifth aspiration, and it has now been fulfilled for me.
Formerly, venerable sir, when I was a prince, I had these five aspirations, and they have now been fulfilled for me.
Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir!

"Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways.
Therefore, venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."

“May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. And may the Blessed One, venerable sir, together with the community of monks, consent to accept a meal from me tomorrow.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, when that night had passed, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared. He had the time announced to the Blessed One, saying:
"It is time, Bhante; the meal is ready.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha together with a great community of monks—a thousand monks, all of whom were formerly matted-hair ascetics.
Now at that time, Sakka, lord of the devas, having assumed the form of a young brahmin student, went before the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, singing these verses:
“The Tamed One, together with the tamed, the ancient matted-hair ascetics;
The Liberated One, together with those who are liberated.”
With the color of refined gold,
the Blessed One entered Rājagaha;
released, he was accompanied by those who were formerly matted-hair ascetics and were now likewise released.
Completely liberated among those who are completely liberated,
the Blessed One, with the color of refined gold, entered Rājagaha.
Crossed over together with those who have crossed over— the ancient matted-hair ascetics—
and liberated together with those who are liberated;
he is the color of refined gold.
The Blessed One entered Rājagaha,
peaceful among the peaceful, together with the ancient matted-hair ascetics,
liberated among those who were liberated.
The Blessed One, with the color of refined gold, entered Rājagaha;
the Ten-Powered One, who has dwelt for ten years.
The Blessed One, who knows the ten qualities and is endowed with the ten [powers],
entered Rājagaha accompanied by a retinue of one thousand followers.
Having seen Sakka, the lord of the devas, people said this:
“How handsome indeed is this young man! How beautiful indeed is this young man! How pleasing indeed is this young man! Whose young man is he?”
When this was said, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed those people with a verse:
“The wise one who is self-controlled in every way,
pure, and without rival;”
“The Worthy One, the Sugata, is in the world;
I am his attendant.
Then the Blessed One approached the residence of King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, and having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of monks.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, having personally served and satisfied the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard and soft food,
sat down to one side when the Blessed One had finished his meal and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl.
As King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha was sitting there, this thought occurred to him:
“Where indeed might the Blessed One dwell?
It should be neither too far from the village nor too near, well-suited for coming and going,
accessible for people who have need of him, with little bustle by day, and quiet, with little noise and free from people by night.”
"It is secluded from humans, suitable for retreat.
Then it occurred to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
"This Veḷuvana park of ours is neither too far from the village nor too close, and it is well-suited for coming and going."

"It is desirable for people who desire it; it is not crowded by day, and at night it is quiet, with little noise and free from the breath of men, a place secluded from people, private, and suitable for retreat.
What if I were to give the Veḷuvana grove to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha?"
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, taking a golden water-pitcher, poured water over the Blessed One’s hand and said:
“Venerable sir, I give this Veḷuvana pleasure grove to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha.
The Blessed One accepted the monastery.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
Then, on this occasion and in this context, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, a monastery.”
The Discourse on the Meeting with Bimbisāra is concluded.
14. The Discourse on the Going-forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna:
Now at that time, the wanderer Sañcaya was residing in Rājagaha together with a large assembly of wanderers, numbering two hundred and fifty wanderers.
Now at that time, Sāriputta and Moggallāna were practicing the holy life under the wanderer Sañjaya.
They had made this agreement:
"Whoever first attains the Deathless shall inform the other."
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Assaji dressed himself, took his bowl and robe, and entered Rājagaha for alms.
He was inspiring, graceful in his advancing and retreating, in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his bending and stretching;
with downcast eyes, he was perfect in his deportment.
The wanderer Sāriputta saw the Venerable Assaji walking for alms in Rājagaha, inspiring confidence in his advancing and retreating,
in his looking ahead and looking aside, in his drawing in and extending of his limbs;
with downcast eyes and perfected in deportment.
Seeing him, it occurred to him:
"Those in the world who are arahants or have entered the path to arahantship—this bhikkhu is surely one of them.
What if I were to approach this bhikkhu and ask him?"
“Friend, for whose sake have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Or whose Dhamma do you approve?
Then it occurred to the wanderer Sāriputta:
“It is not the right time to question this bhikkhu; he has entered among the houses and is walking for alms.”
"What if I were to follow this bhikkhu closely behind, following the path pointed out by those who seek it?
Then the Venerable Assaji, having walked for alms in Rājagaha and taken his almsfood, set out on his way back.

The wanderer Sāriputta then approached the Venerable Assaji; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Assaji, and after exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, the wanderer Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Assaji:
“Your faculties are serene, friend; the color of your skin is purified and bright.
On whose account, friend, have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you find pleasing?”

“Friends, there is a Great Ascetic, a son of the Sakyans who went forth from the Sakyan clan; it was with reference to that Blessed One that I went forth. That Blessed One is my teacher, and I find delight in the Dhamma of that Blessed One.
“But what does your venerable teacher say, friend? What does he proclaim?
