“Friends, I am new, having recently gone forth and only lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline. I am not able to teach the Dhamma in detail; however, I shall speak to you of the meaning in brief.”
Then the wanderer Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Assaji:
"Enough, friend;
whether you speak little or much,"
Tell me only the meaning;
I have need only of the meaning.
What will you do with many words?
Then the Venerable Assaji explained this discourse on Dhamma to the wanderer Sāriputta:
"Of those phenomena that arise from a cause,
the Tathāgata has stated their cause."
“And their cessation—
the Great Ascetic teaches thus. Then,
upon hearing this discourse on the Dhamma, the wanderer Sāriputta attained the dustless, stainless eye of the Dhamma.
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
“If this very Dhamma were realized right then and there,
the stainless state would have been attained.”
“Never seen before, passed away for many hundreds of thousands of eons.
Then the wanderer Sāriputta approached the wanderer Moggallāna.
The wanderer Moggallāna saw the wanderer Sāriputta coming from afar; seeing him, he said this to the wanderer Sāriputta:
“Your faculties are serene, friend, and the color of your skin is purified and bright.
Have you perhaps attained the Deathless, friend?”
“Yes, friend, I have attained the Deathless.
“But how, friend, have you attained the Deathless?
“Here, friend, I saw the bhikkhu Assaji walking for alms in Rājagaha with inspiring deportment.”
With his gaze lowered, he was perfect in his deportment in his every movement—whether stepping back, looking forward, looking aside, drawing in his limbs, or stretching them out.
Seeing him, this thought occurred to me:
"Those in the world who are Arhats, or those who have entered the path to Arhatship—this monk is surely one among them."
"What if I were to approach this bhikkhu and ask him:
'Friend, for whose sake have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Or whose Dhamma do you find pleasing?'?
Then, friends, this occurred to me:
"It is not the right time to question this monk; he has entered among the houses and is walking for alms. Suppose I were to follow closely behind this monk along the path prepared by those in need.
Then, friends, the monk Assaji, having walked for alms in Rājagaha and taken his almsfood, set out on his way back.
Then, friends, I approached the bhikkhu Assaji; having approached, I exchanged greetings with the bhikkhu Assaji, and after exchanging polite and courteous conversation, I stood to one side.
Standing to one side, friends, I said this to the bhikkhu Assaji:
"Your faculties are serene, friend, and the color of your skin is pure and bright."
“Under whom have you gone forth, friend? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you approve?

“There is, friend, a Great Ascetic, a son of the Sakyans who has gone forth from the Sakyan clan; it is under that Blessed One that I have gone forth. That Blessed One is my teacher, and I approve of the Dhamma of that Blessed One.
“But what does your venerable teacher say? What does he proclaim?”
“‘Friend, I am new, having recently gone forth and only lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline; I am not able to teach the Dhamma in detail, but I shall speak to you of its meaning in brief.
Then, friend, I said this to the bhikkhu Assaji:
‘Let it be so, friend.’”
Speak either little or much,
but speak only what is meaningful to me;
for it is meaning alone that I seek.
“What will you do with many words?
Then, friends, the bhikkhu Assaji recited this Dhamma exposition:
“Of those phenomena that arise from a cause...”
“The Tathāgata has declared their cause,
and also their cessation;
such is the teaching of the Great Recluse.”
Then, upon hearing this discourse on the Dhamma, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma arose in the wanderer Moggallāna:
"Whatever is subject to origination, all that is subject to cessation.
This very Dhamma was [realized] by him at that very moment.
The sorrowless lotus has been reached—
unseen and passed beyond by many hundreds of thousands of eons.
Then the wanderer Moggallāna said this to the wanderer Sāriputta:
“Friend, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One; he is our Teacher.
“Friend, these two hundred and fifty wanderers are living here depending on us and looking to us; let us first take leave of them as well.”
“They will do exactly as they think.
Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached those wanderers; having approached them, they said this to those wanderers:
“Friends, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One; that Blessed One is our teacher.”

“Relying upon the venerable ones and looking toward the venerable ones, we dwell here. If the venerable ones will lead the holy life under the Great Recluse, then all of us together shall lead the holy life under the Great Recluse.
Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached the wanderer Sañjaya; having approached, they said this to the wanderer Sañjaya:
“Friend, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One; that Blessed One is our teacher.”
“Enough, friend; do not go. All three of us together shall lead this group.
A second time...
and a third time, Sāriputta and Moggallāna said this to the wanderer Sañjaya:
“Friend, let us go into the presence of the Blessed One; that Blessed One is our teacher.
“Enough, friend, do not go. All three of us together shall lead this group.
Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna, taking those two hundred and fifty wanderers with them, approached Veḷuvana.
But as for the wanderer Sañcaya, warm blood gushed from his mouth right there.
The Blessed One saw Sāriputta and Moggallāna coming from afar; having seen them, he addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, those two companions are coming—Kolita and Upatissa."
“This shall be my pair of disciples, the foremost, the auspicious pair,” [he said] regarding the profound sphere of knowledge,
the unsurpassed destruction of the substrata of existence.
When they had arrived at Veḷuvana,
the Teacher then declared concerning them:
"These two companions..."
"Kolita and Upatissa are coming;
this pair of disciples shall be my foremost auspicious pair."
Then Sāriputta and Moggallāna approached the Blessed One; having approached, they prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and said this to him:
“Venerable sir, may we receive the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive the full admission.
“Come, monks,” the Blessed One said.
“The Dhamma is well-expounded; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering.
That itself was the full ordination of those venerable ones.
14.1. The Going-forth of the Well-Known Ones.
Now at that time, many well-known young men of good family from Magadha were leading the holy life under the Blessed One.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"The ascetic Gotama practices for the sake of sonlessness; the ascetic Gotama practices for the sake of widowhood; the ascetic Gotama practices for the destruction of families."
"The ascetic Gotama is practicing rightly; now he has ordained a thousand matted-hair ascetics, and these two hundred and fifty wanderers of the Sañjaya group have also been ordained.
Furthermore, these well-known and distinguished sons of noble families from Magadha are leading the holy life under the ascetic Gotama."
Moreover, seeing the monks, they reproved them with this verse:
"The Great Recluse has arrived at Giribbaja of the Magadhans."
“Having led everyone away to their accumulation,
whom will he lead now?
The bhikkhus heard those people complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One...
"Bhikkhus, that sound will not last long; it will last for only seven days, and after the passing of seven days, it will disappear.
Therefore, bhikkhus, as for those who reproach you with this verse—"
“The Great Ascetic has arrived at Giribbaja of the Magadhans;
having led all [the people] to Sañcaya, ...”
"Who now will lead Kaṁsa away?
You should then challenge them with this verse:
"The Great Heroes indeed lead [others] away..."
“The Tathāgatas [teach] by means of the true Dhamma;
for those who lead by the Dhamma,
what envy can there be among those who understand?”
Now at that time, when people saw the bhikkhus, they reproached them with this verse:
“The Great Ascetic has arrived at Giribbaja of the Magadhans;”
“Having led everyone away into accumulation,
whom will he lead now?
Thus the monks rebuked those people with this verse.
“Indeed, the Great Heroes,
the Tathāgatas, lead by means of the True Dhamma; for those who lead by means of the Dhamma, [there is no fear].”
"What envy can there be for those who understand?

Thus it was that people said, "It seems the ascetics, sons of the Sakyan, lead by the Dhamma and not by what is not the Dhamma. That report lasted for only seven days; at the end of seven days, it vanished.
The account of the going forth of Sāriputta and Moggallāna is finished.
The fourth recitation section is finished.
15. Discussion on the Duties toward a Preceptor.
Now at that time, monks who were without preceptors and without teachers, being neither exhorted nor instructed, went for alms with poorly dressed and poorly clad bodies, lacking in proper decorum.
While people were eating, they would hold out an empty bowl even over the food being consumed;
they would hold out an empty bowl even over the hard foods; they would hold out an empty bowl even over the soft foods;
and they would hold out an empty bowl even over the drinks.
They requested soft drinks, soups, and boiled rice, and ate them;
they also stayed in the dining hall making loud noises and great clamor.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can the recluses, sons of the Sakyans, wander for alms poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum? While people are eating,
they will hold out their bowls even over the food being served, they will hold out their bowls even over the hard food being served,
they will hold out their bowls even over the soft food being served, and they will hold out their bowls even over the drinks being served.”
"They will hold out their bowls to receive food;
they will request curry and rice for themselves and eat it;
and they will dwell making loud noises and great clamor in the dining hall, just like brahmins at a brahminical feast."
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Those monks who were of few desires, contented, modest, scrupulous, and desirous of training, grumbled, complained, and criticized:
"How can these monks go for alms poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum?"
While people are eating, they will hold out an empty bowl even when there is more food to be served;
they will hold out an empty bowl even when there is more hard food to be served; they will hold out an empty bowl even when there is more soft food to be served;
they will hold out an empty bowl even when there is more drink to be served.
“They will request rice porridge and boiled rice with curry and eat them;
they will also dwell in the dining hall making loud noises and great clamor. Then those bhikkhus... [as before]... Please provide the text you would like me to translate. I am ready to assist you.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this context, having convened the community of monks, questioned the monks:
"Is it true, monks, that monks are walking for alms poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum?"
While people were eating, they would hold out an empty bowl even for the food being served above;

they would hold out an empty bowl even for the hard foods being served above; they would hold out an empty bowl even for the soft foods being served above; they would hold out an empty bowl even for the drinks being served above;
and they would eat by having curry and rice requested for themselves right there in the dining hall.
“Do they dwell making loud noises and great clamor?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them.
“Monks, it is unseemly for those foolish men, it is improper, unsuitable, unworthy of a recluse, unbecoming, and not to be done.
How indeed, monks, can those foolish men wander for alms poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in decorum;
how can they hold out their bowls even above the food while people are eating?
They will offer their bowls when the solid food has already been finished; they will offer their bowls when the soft food has already been finished;
they will offer their bowls when the drinking water has already been finished; they will eat after having themselves requested both curry and rice;
and they will dwell in the dining hall making loud noises and great clamor.
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence, nor to the increase of confidence in those who already have it.
On the contrary, monks, this leads to the lack of confidence in those without confidence, and to the alienation of some of those who already have confidence.
Then the Blessed One, having rebuked those monks in many ways for their being difficult to support and difficult to maintain...
Having spoken in many ways on the dispraise of great desire, lack of contentment, socializing, and laziness,
and having spoken in many ways on the praise of being easy to support, easy to satisfy, of fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement, the ascetic qualities, serenity,
reduction of worldly things, and the arousal of energy, he spoke to the monks what was suitable and appropriate for them.
Having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, a preceptor.
A preceptor, bhikkhus, should maintain a mind toward his co-resident like that of a father; a co-resident should maintain a mind toward his preceptor like that of a son.”
In this way, living with mutual respect, deference, and harmonious conduct, they will attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
And furthermore, monks, a preceptor is to be taken in this manner:
having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at his feet, having sat down on one’s heels and extended the joined palms in reverential salutation, he should speak to him thus:
“Venerable sir, be my preceptor;
venerable sir, be my preceptor;
venerable sir, be my preceptor.”

If one makes a request by body, by speech, or by both body and speech—saying "It is good," or "It is easy," or "It is appropriate," or "It is fitting," or "Please accomplish it with a pleasing manner"—then the preceptor is accepted.
If one does not make a request by body, nor by speech, nor by both body and speech, then the preceptor is not accepted.
Monks, a co-resident student must conduct himself properly toward his preceptor.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
having risen early, removing one's sandals, and arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, one should provide a tooth-stick, provide water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat.
If there is conjey, one should wash the vessel and offer the conjey.
Having given water to one who has drunk the gruel, and having received the vessel, he should wash it carefully without scratching it, keeping it low, and then put it away.
When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be lifted up.
If that place is dirty, that place should be swept.

If the preceptor wishes to enter a village, the inner robe should be given to him; the outer robe should be received back; the waistband should be given; the upper robes should be handed over after folding them in layers; and the bowl should be washed and given back with water for rinsing.

If the preceptor desires an attendant, [the pupil] should cover the three circles, put on the lower robe evenly, fasten the waistband, fold the upper robes in layers and put them on, and fasten the toggle.
Having washed the bowl and taken it, one should act as the attendant monk behind the preceptor.
One should not walk too far away, nor too close; one should receive whatever is placed in the bowl.
One should not interrupt the preceptor’s speech with talk in between.
If the preceptor speaks concerning an offense, he should be restrained.
As he returns, [the pupil] should arrive first, prepare a seat, set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone;
he should go out to meet him and receive his bowl and robe, and give him a lower garment.
The lower robe should be accepted.
If the robe is damp, it should be dried in the sun for a short while, but the robe must not be left in the sun;
the robe should be folded, and when folding the robe, one should fold it after turning back a four-finger-width of the edge.
"Lest there be a breakage in the middle," he said.
"The waistband should be fastened around the body.
If there is almsfood and the preceptor wishes to eat, one should give him water and then offer the almsfood."
The preceptor should be asked for water.

Having given water to one who has finished eating, he should receive the bowl, hold it low, wash it carefully without scratching it, dry it, and let it warm for a short while in the heat; however, the bowl must not be placed directly in the heat.
The bowl and robes should then be set aside.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand, touch the area beneath the bed or beneath the bench with the other hand, and then set down the bowl.
Furthermore, the bowl must not be set down on the bare ground.

When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the outer side and the fold toward the inner side, and then set down the robe.
When the preceptor has risen, the seat should be put away; the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-stand should be set aside.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.
If the preceptor wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared.
If there is need for cold, cold should be prepared.
If there is need for heat, heat should be prepared.
If the preceptor wishes to enter the sauna, powder should be kneaded and clay moistened.
Taking the sauna-bench, he should follow closely behind his preceptor;
having offered the sauna-bench and received the robe, he should set it aside to one side. He should provide the bath-powder and the clay.
If he is able, he should enter the sauna.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover the front and the back, and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior monks,
nor should one block the junior monks from their seats.
In the sauna, one should perform services for one’s preceptor.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench, cover oneself both in front and behind, and then exit the sauna.
In the water as well, one should perform services for one’s preceptor.
Having bathed first, emerged from the water, dried one's own limbs, and dressed oneself,
one should wipe the water from the preceptor’s body, give him his lower robe, and give him his upper robe. Taking the sauna-bench,
one should return first and prepare a seat, as well as the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-scraper.
The water should be set out, and the preceptor should be asked for water.
If he wishes to have the recitation performed, it should be recited;
if he wishes to ask questions, he should be questioned.
In whatever monastery the preceptor resides, if that monastery is dirty and he is able to do so, it should be cleaned.
When cleaning the monastery, first the bowl and robes should be taken out and placed to one side.
The sitting mat and the rug should be taken out and placed to one side.
Having removed the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side.
Having lowered the bed, one should remove it to one side, taking care not to strike it or to let it brush against the surface of the door.
Having lowered the stool, one should remove it to one side, taking care not to strike it or to let it brush against the surface of the door.
The bed-legs should be removed and placed to one side.
The spittoon should be removed and placed to one side.
The leaning-board should be removed and placed to one side.
Having observed the floor-covering as it was laid out, one should take it away and set it aside to one side.
If there are cobwebs in the dwelling, they should first be removed from the ceiling; the openings for light and the corners should be wiped clean.
If the wall treated with red-ochre plaster has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the ground has been blackened and is dusty, it should be wiped clean after moistening and squeezing out a cloth.
If the ground has not been treated, it should be sprinkled with water and swept, thinking:
"Lest the monastery be covered in dust."
Having sifted through the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
Having aired out the floor-covering, cleaned it, beaten it, and brought it back, it should be spread out as it was previously arranged.
Having aired out the bed-legs, wiped them, and brought them back, they should be placed in their proper position.
Having aired out the bed, cleaned it, dusted it, lowered it, and carefully carried it in without scraping it or knocking against the door frame, one should set it out in its assigned place.
Having aired out the chair, cleaned it, dusted it, lowered it, and carefully carried it in without scraping it or knocking against the door frame, one should set it out in its assigned place.
Having aired out the mattress and pillow, cleaned them, and dusted them, one should carry them in and set them out in their assigned places.
The sitting mat and the rug should be dried in the sun, cleaned, beaten, brought back inside, and spread out as they were previously arranged.
The spittoon should be dried in the sun, wiped clean, brought back inside, and placed in its proper place.
The leaning board should be dried in the sun, wiped clean, brought back inside, and placed in its proper place.
The bowl and robes must be set aside.
When setting aside the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, touch the space beneath the bed or beneath the seat, and then set the bowl down.
The bowl must not be set down on the bare ground.

When putting away the robe-cloth, one should take hold of the cloth with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, and then put it away.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the west, the western windows should be closed.
If dust-laden winds blow from the north, the northern windows should be closed.
If dust-laden winds blow from the south, the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold, the windows should be opened by day and closed at night.
If it is hot weather, the windows should be closed by day and opened at night.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse should be swept.
If the assembly hall is dirty, the assembly hall should be swept.
If the fire-hall is dirty, the fire-hall should be swept.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If drinking water is not available, drinking water should be provided.
If bathing water is not available, bathing water should be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing pitcher, the rinsing pitcher should be filled with water.
If dissatisfaction arises in the preceptor, it should be dispelled by the student, or he should cause it to be dispelled, or a discourse on the Dhamma should be given to him.
If remorse arises in the preceptor, it should be removed by the student, or he should cause it to be removed, or a discourse on the Dhamma should be given to him.
If a wrong view arises in the preceptor, it should be cleared away by the student, or he should cause it to be cleared away, or a discourse on the Dhamma should be given to him.
If the preceptor has committed a heavy offense and is subject to probation, the student living with him should make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha grant probation to my preceptor?
If the preceptor is subject to being sent back to the beginning, the student living with him should make an effort...
"How might the Saṅgha send the preceptor back to the beginning?
If the preceptor is deserving of the *mānatta* discipline, the student living with him should make an effort:
"How might the Saṅgha grant the *mānatta* discipline to the preceptor?"
If the preceptor is deserving of rehabilitation, the student living with him should make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha rehabilitate my preceptor?

If the Saṅgha intends to carry out a formal act against the preceptor—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the student living with him should make an effort.
"How might the Saṅgha not perform a formal act against my preceptor, or how might it transform a heavy one into a light one?

Or, if a formal act has already been performed against him by the Saṅgha—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the student living with him should make an effort:
"How might my preceptor conduct himself properly, behave with humility, and act so as to bring about his own rehabilitation, such that the Saṅgha might revoke that formal act?"
If the preceptor’s robe needs washing, it should be washed by the student, or he should make an effort, thinking:
“How can my preceptor’s robe be washed?
If the preceptor’s robe needs making, it should be made by the student, or he should make an effort.
"How indeed should the preceptor’s robe be prepared?
If the preceptor’s dye needs to be boiled, it should be boiled by the student, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How indeed can the preceptor’s dye be boiled?"
If the preceptor’s robe needs dyeing, it should be dyed by the student, or he should make an effort, thinking:
“How can my preceptor’s robe be dyed?
When dyeing the robe, he should dye it carefully, turning it over repeatedly; he must not leave while the drops of dye have not yet dried.
Without having asked one's preceptor for permission, one should not give an almsbowl to anyone, nor should one receive an almsbowl from anyone;
one should not give a robe to anyone, nor should one receive a robe from anyone;
one should not give requisites to anyone, nor should one receive requisites from anyone.
One should not have one person's hair cut, nor should one have another person's hair cut;
one should not perform service for one person, nor should one have service performed by another;
one should not do a favor for one person, nor should one have a favor done for another.
One should not act as an attendant for anyone else, nor should one accept anyone as an attendant;
one should not have almsfood brought out for anyone else, nor should one have anyone bring out almsfood;
one should not enter a village without having asked permission from one’s preceptor.
One should not go to a cemetery;
one should not depart for distant regions.
If one’s preceptor is ill, he should be attended to for as long as life lasts.
“His recovery must be awaited.
The Duties Toward the Preceptor are finished.
16. Discussion of the Duties Toward the Co-resident Disciple.
“Monks, the preceptor should behave properly toward his co-resident.
In this regard, this is proper behavior:
Monks, the preceptor should support and assist the co-resident with recitation, interrogation, exhortation, and instruction.”
If the preceptor has a bowl but the resident pupil does not have a bowl, the preceptor should give his bowl to the resident pupil, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How can a bowl be obtained for the resident pupil?

If the preceptor has a robe but the resident pupil does not have a robe, the preceptor should give his robe to the resident pupil, or he should make an effort— [thinking: "How can a robe be obtained for the resident pupil?"]
"How might a robe accrue for the student?
If the preceptor has requisites but the student does not have requisites, the preceptor should give requisites to the student, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How might requisites accrue for the student?"
If the co-resident student is ill, having risen early, one should give him a tooth-stick, provide water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat.
If there is rice-gruel, one should wash the vessel and offer the gruel to him.
After he has drunk the gruel, one should give him water, receive the vessel, hold it low, and wash it carefully without scraping it, then put it away.
When the student has risen, the seat should be lifted up.
If that place is dirty, that place should be swept.
If the student wishes to enter the village, the lower robe should be given to him and the upper robe received back.
The waistband should be given; the outer robes should be given after being folded; the bowl should be washed and given with water for rinsing.
Thinking, "He will turn back at this point," a seat should be prepared; water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-stand should be set out;
one should go out to meet him and receive his bowl and robes; and an inner robe should be given.
The lower robe should be accepted.
If the robe is damp, it should be dried in the sun for a short time, but the robe must not be left in the sun;
the robe should be folded, and when folding the robe, one should fold it with the edges turned back four finger-widths.
"Lest there be a breakage in the middle," he thought.
He should fasten the waist-band around his body.
If there is almsfood and the student (saddhivihārika) wishes to eat, he should give him water and offer the almsfood to him.
The co-resident student should be asked if he has had enough water to drink.

After the teacher has finished eating, the student should give him water, receive his bowl, hold it low, wash it carefully without scratching it, dry it thoroughly, and let it warm for a short while in the heat; however, the bowl must not be left out in the heat.
He should then put away the bowl and the robes.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, touch the lower part of the bed or the lower part of the seat before setting the bowl down.
The bowl must not be set down on the ground that has not been cleared of dust.

When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand and, with the other hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string; then, having arranged the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, the robe should be put away.
When the student has risen, the seat should be lifted up; the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-stand should be put away.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.
If the student wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared.
If there is need for cold, cold should be prepared.
If there is need for warmth, warmth should be prepared.
If the student living with him wishes to enter the sauna, powder should be kneaded and clay moistened.
Taking the sauna-bench, he should go and give the sauna-bench [to the resident], receive the robe, and set it aside to one side.
He should provide bath-powder and clay.
If he is able, he should enter the sauna.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover both the front and the back, and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon senior bhikkhus,
nor should one block junior bhikkhus from their seats.
In the sauna, one should perform services for one’s co-resident student.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench, cover oneself both in front and behind, and then exit the sauna.
In the water as well, one should perform services for one’s co-resident student.
Having bathed first, emerged from the water, dried his limbs, and put on his lower robe, he should wipe the water from his student’s body, give him his lower robe, and give him his upper robe.
Taking the sauna-bench, he should return first, arrange a seat, and set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-wiping cloth.
He should ask the student if he wants drinking water.
In whatever dwelling his student lives, if that dwelling is dirty, it should be cleaned if he is able.
When cleaning the dwelling, first the bowl and robes should be taken out and placed to one side;
the sitting mat and the spread should be taken out and placed to one side.
Having removed the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side.
Having lowered the bed, one should remove it and place it to one side, taking care not to strike it or to let it brush against the surface of the door.
Having lowered the bench, one should remove it and place it to one side, taking care not to strike it or to let it brush against the surface of the door.
The bed-legs should be removed and placed to one side;
the spittoon should be removed and placed to one side;
the leaning-board should be removed and placed to one side.
Having observed the floor-covering as it was laid out, one should take it away and set it aside to one side.
If there is a crack in the dwelling, the ceiling should first be removed; the light-shafts, corners, and edges should be wiped clean.
If the wall has been treated with red ocher and is moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the ground has been blackened and is dusty, it should be wiped clean with a cloth that has been soaked and wrung out.
If the ground has not been treated, it should be sprinkled with water and swept, thinking:
"May the monastery not be covered in dust."
Having sifted through the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
Having aired out the floor-covering, cleaned it, and beaten it, and having brought it back, it should be spread out as it was previously arranged.
Having aired out the bed-legs, wiped them, and brought them back, they should be placed in their proper positions.

Having dried the bed in the sun, cleaned it, tapped it, lowered it, and having brought it back carefully without scratching it or knocking it against the surface of the door, one should arrange it in its proper place.

Having dried the chair in the sun, cleaned it, tapped it, lowered it, and having brought it back carefully without scratching it or knocking it against the surface of the door, one should arrange it in its proper place.
Having dried the mattress and pillow in the sun, cleaned them, and tapped them, one should bring them back and arrange them in their proper places.
The sitting mat and the rug should be dried in the sun, cleaned, beaten to remove dust, brought back inside, and spread out as they were previously arranged.
The spittoon should be dried in the sun, wiped clean, brought back inside, and placed in its proper place.
The leaning board should be dried in the sun, wiped clean, brought back inside, and placed in its proper place.
The bowl and robes must be set down.
When setting down the bowl, one should grasp the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, touch the lower part of the bed or the lower part of the seat, and then set down the bowl.
The bowl must not be set down on the bare ground.

When putting away the robe-clothing, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, and then put it away.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the west, the western windows should be closed.
If dust-laden winds blow from the north, the northern windows should be closed.
If dust-laden winds blow from the south, the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold, the windows should be opened during the day and closed at night.
If it is hot, the windows should be closed by day and opened at night.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse should be swept.
If the assembly hall is dirty, the assembly hall should be swept.
If the fire-hall is dirty, the fire-hall should be swept.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If drinking water is not available, drinking water should be provided.
If washing water is not available, washing water should be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, the rinsing-pitcher should be filled with water.

If dissatisfaction arises in the student, the preceptor should dispel it, have it dispelled, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma. If anxiety arises in the student, the preceptor should remove it, have it removed, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If a wrong view arises in the student, the preceptor should separate him from it, have him separated from it, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If a co-resident student has committed a heavy offense (garudhamma) and is subject to probation, the preceptor must make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha grant probation to this co-resident student?
If a co-resident student is subject to being sent back to the beginning, the preceptor must make an effort...
"How might the Saṅgha send the student back to the beginning?
If the student is deserving of the *mānatta* penance, the preceptor must make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha grant the *mānatta* penance to the student?"
If the student living with him is deserving of rehabilitation, the preceptor must make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Sangha rehabilitate the student living with me?

If the Sangha intends to perform a formal act against the student living with him—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the preceptor must make an effort.
"How might the Saṅgha not carry out a formal act against the student, or how might it transform a heavy one into a light one?

Furthermore, if a formal act has been carried out against him by the Saṅgha—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the preceptor should make an effort, thinking:
"How might the student conduct himself properly, behave with humility, and act in a way that leads to his release, so that the Saṅgha might revoke that formal act?"
If the robe-cloth of a student needs washing, the preceptor should either instruct him, "Wash it in this way," or make an effort, thinking,
"How can the student's robe-cloth be washed?
If the robe-cloth of a student needs making, the preceptor should either instruct him, "Make it in this way," or make an effort.
"How, then, should the robe of a student be prepared?
If the student’s dye needs to be boiled, the preceptor should instruct him, "Boil it in this way," or he should make an effort,
thinking, "How can the student’s dye be boiled?"
If a student’s robe needs dyeing, the preceptor must either give instructions, saying, “Dye it thus,” or make an effort,
thinking, “How can the student’s robe be dyed?
When dyeing the robe, it should be turned over carefully again and again while being dyed.
And one should not depart while the drops are still falling.
If the student is ill, he should attend him for as long as life lasts; he should wait for his recovery.
Thus ends the duties toward a student.
17. The Discourse on Expulsion.
Now at that time, the students did not conduct themselves properly toward their preceptors.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... were indignant, complained, and became vexed, saying:
“How indeed can the students not behave properly toward their preceptors?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One. … [The Buddha asked:
“Is it true, monks, that the students do not behave properly toward their preceptors?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How indeed, monks, can students not conduct themselves properly toward their preceptors? …” [and so on].
Having rebuked him … and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Monks, a student must not fail to behave properly toward his preceptor.”
“Whoever does not conduct themselves properly commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Yet they did not conduct themselves properly.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to dismiss one who does not conduct himself properly.
And in this way, monks, he should be dismissed:
by saying ‘I dismiss you,’ or ‘Do not stay here,’ or ‘Take away your bowl and robe,’ or ‘I am not…”
‘He should be attended by her’— if he makes this known by body, or makes it known by speech,
or makes it known by both body and speech, the student has been dismissed;
if he does not make it known by body, nor make it known by speech, nor make it known by both body and speech, the student has not been dismissed.”
Now at that time, the students who had been dismissed were not asking for forgiveness.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to ask for forgiveness,” he said.
They did not ask for forgiveness.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one who has been expelled must not fail to ask for forgiveness.”
“Whoever does not ask for forgiveness commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, preceptors, when being asked for forgiveness, would not forgive.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to forgive,” [the Blessed One said].
Yet they did not forgive.
Consequently, the co-residents would depart, disrobe, or even go over to other sects.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who is being asked for forgiveness must grant it.
Whoever does not grant forgiveness commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, preceptors were dismissing those who were conducting themselves properly, but not dismissing those who were not conducting themselves properly.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one who is conducting himself properly should not be dismissed.”
Whoever should dismiss him, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
And, monks, one who does not behave properly must not be dismissed.
Whoever should not dismiss him, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
“Monks, a student who possesses five qualities should be dismissed.

He has no excessive affection for his preceptor; he has no excessive confidence in him; he has no excessive sense of shame before him; he has no excessive respect for him; he has no excessive devotion toward him.
Monks, a student who possesses these five qualities should be dismissed.”
“Monks, a student who possesses five qualities should not be dismissed.
He has excessive affection for his preceptor, he has excessive confidence in him, he has excessive moral shame, he has excessive reverence for him, and he has excessive devotion toward him.
Monks, a student possessing these five qualities should not be dismissed.”
“Monks, a student endowed with five qualities is fit to be dismissed.
He has no excessive affection for his preceptor; he has no excessive confidence in him; he has no excessive sense of shame; he has no excessive reverence for him;
he has no excessive devotion toward him. Monks, a student endowed with these five qualities is fit to be dismissed.”
“Monks, a student who possesses five qualities is not fit to be dismissed.

He has excessive affection for his preceptor; he has excessive confidence in him; he has excessive moral shame; he has excessive reverence for him; and he has excessive devotion to spiritual development.
Monks, a student possessing these five qualities is not fit to be dismissed.”
“Monks, when a preceptor possesses five qualities, he is at fault if he does not dismiss his co-resident disciple, but he is not at fault if he dismisses him.

He has no excessive affection for the preceptor; he has no excessive confidence in the preceptor; he has no excessive sense of shame before the preceptor; he has no excessive reverence for the preceptor;

he has no excessive devotion toward the preceptor. Monks, when a co-resident disciple possesses these five qualities, the preceptor is at fault if he does not dismiss him, but he is not at fault if he dismisses him.”
“Monks, when a preceptor sends away a student who possesses five qualities, he is at fault; when he does not send him away, he is not at fault.
There is excessive affection for the preceptor, excessive confidence in the preceptor, excessive moral shame, excessive reverence for the preceptor, and excessive devotion toward the preceptor.
Monks, when a student possesses these five qualities, the preceptor who sends him away is at fault; the one who does not send him away is not at fault.”
Now at that time, a certain brahmin approached some monks and requested the going forth.
The monks did not wish to grant him the going forth.
Not obtaining the going forth among the monks, he became emaciated, haggard, discolored, and pale, with his veins showing all over his body.
The Blessed One saw that brahmin—emaciated, haggard, discolored, jaundiced, and with veins showing all over his body. Having seen him, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, why is that brahmin emaciated, haggard, discolored, jaundiced, and with veins showing all over his body?
“Venerable sir, that brahmin approached the bhikkhus and requested the going forth.”
The monks did not wish to give him the going-forth.
Not obtaining the going-forth among the monks, he became emaciated, haggard, discolored, jaundiced, and his veins were visible all over his body.
Then the Blessed One addressed the monks:
“Monks, who among you remembers a service rendered by that brahmin?
When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One:
“I, Bhante, remember a service rendered by that brahmin.”
“But, Sāriputta, do you remember a service rendered by that brahmin?
“Venerable sir, here that brahmin had a spoonful of almsfood given to me as I was walking for alms in Rājagaha.
Venerable sir, I remember this service rendered by that brahmin.”
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta! For noble persons, Sāriputta, are grateful and appreciative.
Therefore, Sāriputta, let that brahmin go forth and receive full ordination.
“But how, Bhante, shall I have that brahmin go forth and receive full ordination?”
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with regard to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, that ordination by the three goings for refuge which was authorized by me, I rescind from this day forward.
I authorize you, bhikkhus, to confer ordination by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.”
And furthermore, monks, he should be ordained in this way:
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me.
This person, named so-and-so, desires full ordination from the Venerable named so-and-so.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant full ordination to this person, with so-and-so as preceptor.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
This person named so-and-so desires the full ordination from the venerable one named so-and-so.
The Sangha grants the full ordination to so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor."
Whichever venerable one approves of the full ordination of [name] with [name] as preceptor, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
A second time I state this matter: [same as above].
Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
This person named so-and-so desires the full ordination from the venerable one named so-and-so.
The Sangha grants the full ordination to so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor.
Whichever venerable one approves of the full ordination of [Name] with [Name] as preceptor, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
For the third time I state this matter:
Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
This person named so-and-so desires the full ordination from the venerable one named so-and-so.
The Sangha grants the full ordination to so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor.
Whichever venerable one approves of the full ordination of [Name] with [Name] as preceptor, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
[Name] has been fully ordained by the Sangha with [Name] as preceptor.
“It is agreeable to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, immediately after being ordained, engaged in improper conduct.
The bhikkhus said this:
“Friend, do not do such a thing; this is not allowable.
He replied, “I did not ask the venerable ones, ‘Please ordain me.’”
"Why have you ordained me without being asked?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, one should not ordain someone without being asked."
Whoever should confer full ordination [without being requested], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, I allow you to confer full ordination when one has been requested.
And thus, monks, should one be requested.

That person seeking full ordination, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the bhikkhus, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, I request full ordination from the Saṅgha; may the Saṅgha, out of compassion, lift me up.
He should request a second time as well.
A third time he should be asked.
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me."
This person, named so-and-so, desires full ordination from the Venerable named so-and-so.
Named so-and-so requests full ordination from the Saṅgha with named so-and-so as preceptor.
If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant full ordination to named so-and-so with named so-and-so as preceptor.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
This person named so-and-so desires the full ordination from the venerable one named so-and-so.
The one named so-and-so requests full ordination from the Sangha with so-and-so as preceptor.
The Sangha grants full ordination to so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor.
Whosoever among the venerable ones approves of the full ordination of so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve of this, let him speak.
A second time I state this matter...
[as before] ...A third time I state this matter... [as before].
“[He has been] ordained by the Saṅgha, [he who is] so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent; thus do I understand this.
Now at that time, in Rājagaha, a rotation for the distribution of choice meals had been established.
Then a certain brahmin thought to himself:
"These ascetics, sons of the Sakyans, are easy in their conduct and easy in their behavior; having eaten fine food, they sleep on beds sheltered from the wind.
What if I were to go forth among the ascetics, the sons of the Sakyans?"
Then that brahmin approached the monks and requested the going-forth.
The monks granted him the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon him.
Once he had gone forth, the turn for meals was exhausted.
The bhikkhus said,
"Come now, friend, let us go for alms.
He replied:
“I did not go forth for this reason, friend, thinking, ‘I will wander for alms.
If you give to me, I will eat; if you do not give to me, I will disrobe.
“But, friend, have you gone forth for the sake of your belly?”
“Indeed, friends,” they replied.
Then those monks who were few in desires... [as before]... were indignant, disparaged this, and complained:
“How can a monk, in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya, go forth for the sake of his belly?”
Those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ...“Is it true, bhikkhu, that you went forth for the sake of your stomach?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, go forth for the sake of the belly in such a well-expounded Dhamma and Vinaya?
This, foolish man, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of those with faith…” [and so on].
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, bhikkhus, for one who is conferring full ordination, to explain the four requisites.”
Going forth is dependent upon subsisting on alms-food; in this regard, you should make an effort for as long as life lasts.
Additional gains include:
meals provided by the Saṅgha, designated meals, invitations, tickets for meals, fortnightly meals, Uposatha-day meals, and meals on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
Going forth is dependent upon rag-robes; you should make an effort regarding this for as long as life lasts.
Any extra acquisitions are:
linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and bark-fiber cloth.
Going forth is dependent on the lodging at the foot of a tree; there you should exert yourself for as long as life lasts.
Any additional gain consists of:
a monastery, a gabled house, a multi-storied building, a mansion, or a cave.
"Going forth by means of fermented urine as medicine: you should exert yourself in this for as long as life lasts.
Any extra gain consists of ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses."
The fifth section on the duties toward the preceptor is finished.
18. Discussion of the Duties Toward the Teacher:
Now at that time, a certain young brahmin approached the bhikkhus and requested the going-forth.
The monks explained the supports to him beforehand.
He said this:
"Venerable sirs, if you had explained the supports to me before I went forth, I would have remained here."
“Venerable sir, I will not go forth;
my dwelling-places are loathsome and repulsive to me.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, dependence should not be assigned beforehand.
Whoever should assign it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, I allow that dependence be assigned immediately after one has been fully ordained.”
Now at that time, monks were conferring full ordination by a group of even two or three.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one should not confer full ordination by a group of fewer than ten.”
"Whoever should confer full ordination [on someone less than ten years senior], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
I allow you, monks, to confer full ordination by a group of ten or a group of more than ten.
Now at that time, monks who had been ordained for only one year or two years were conferring full ordination on their co-residents.
The Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, having been ordained for one year, gave the full ordination to a student.

Having completed his rains retreat, being now two years ordained, he took that student—who had been ordained for one year—and approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
Now it is the custom for the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, to exchange greetings with visiting monks.
Then the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta:
“Bhikkhu, I hope you are bearing up; I hope you are getting by;
I hope you have come along the road without too much fatigue?”
“It is bearable, Blessed One; it is sustainable, Blessed One.
We have come along this road, Bhante, without much fatigue.
Though Tathāgatas know [the answer], they ask; though they know, they do not ask. They ask when they perceive the right time; they do not ask when they perceive the right time.
The Tathāgatas ask what is connected with the goal, not what is unconnected with the goal.
Regarding what is unconnected with the goal, the Tathāgatas have cut off the bridge.
In two ways do the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, question the bhikkhus: either "We shall teach the Dhamma," or "We shall lay down a training rule for the disciples."
Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Upasena Vaṅgantaputta, “Monk, how many years have you been ordained?
“I am two years ordained, Blessed One.
“And this monk, how many years has he been ordained?”
“One year, Blessed One.
“What is this monk to you?
“He is my co-resident, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“It is unseemly, foolish man, it is unbecoming, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.
How can you, foolish man, having yourself been exhorted and instructed by others, think to exhort and instruct another?”
“Too much, you foolish man, have you turned toward abundance, namely, the binding together of a group.
This, foolish man, does not lead to the inspiring of those without confidence, nor to the increase of those who are already confident...
Having rebuked him... [the Blessed One spoke].”
Having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, one who has fewer than ten years of seniority must not grant full ordination.
Whoever should grant it commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
“I allow you, monks, to grant full ordination when one has ten years of seniority or more than ten years.
At that time, however, the monks [thought], “We have ten years; we have ten years.”
Fools and incompetent persons confer full ordination.
One sees foolish preceptors and wise co-residents;
one sees incompetent preceptors and competent co-residents.
One sees preceptors who are of little learning, while their resident pupils are very learned;
one sees preceptors who lack wisdom, while their resident pupils are wise.

Furthermore, there was one who had formerly been a member of another sect; when he was being addressed by his preceptor in accordance with the Dhamma, he leveled a challenge against his preceptor’s doctrine and returned to that very same sectarian fold.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can these foolish and incompetent bhikkhus give the full admission [thinking], ‘We have ten years of seniority, we have ten years of seniority’?
One sees preceptors who are foolish while their co-residents are wise; one sees preceptors who are incompetent while their co-residents are competent.”
“Skilled preceptors are seen who have little learning while their co-residents are very learned;
preceptors are seen who lack wisdom while their co-residents are wise.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Is it true, monks, that foolish and incompetent monks are giving the full ordination [thinking], ‘We have ten years of seniority, we have ten years of seniority’?”
Are there seen preceptors who are foolish while their co-residents are wise; are there seen preceptors who are incompetent while their co-residents are competent;
are there seen preceptors who have heard little while their co-residents are learned;
are there seen preceptors who lack wisdom while their co-residents possess wisdom?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How can those foolish, incompetent men, thinking ‘I have ten years [of seniority], I have ten years,’ give the full ordination? …”
It is seen that preceptors are foolish while their co-residents are wise; it is seen that preceptors are incompetent while their co-residents are competent;
it is seen that preceptors have little learning while their co-residents are learned;
it is seen that preceptors lack wisdom while their co-residents are possessed of wisdom.
"Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked him...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:"
“Monks, one who is foolish and incompetent should not grant full ordination.
Whoever should grant it commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow a monk who is competent, capable, and has ten years of seniority or more, to grant full ordination.”
Now at that time, when their preceptors had departed, disrobed, died, or joined another faction, the monks were without teachers.
Not being exhorted and not being instructed, they went for alms poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum.
While people were eating, they held out their bowls even over the food already on the table; they held out their bowls even over the hard foods, the soft foods, and the drinks.
They requested and ate both curry and rice by means of conciliation;
they also remained in the dining hall making loud noises and great clamor.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, wander for alms poorly dressed, poorly clad, and lacking in proper decorum?
While people are eating, they will hold out their bowls even over the main course; they will hold out their bowls even over the hard food, the soft food, and the drinks.
They will even request curry and rice for themselves and eat them.”
“They will dwell making loud noises and great clamor even in the refectory, just like brahmins at a brahmin feast.
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and expressing their indignation...
[and so on] ...Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Is it true, monks, that [this is so]?
… “It is true, Blessed One.
… Having rebuked him and given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, a teacher.
Monks, a teacher should maintain toward his pupil the same attitude as a father toward a son; a pupil should maintain toward his teacher the same attitude as a son toward a father.
In this way, living with mutual respect, deference, and harmony, they will attain growth, increase, and abundance in this Dhamma and Vinaya.”
"I allow you, monks, for one who has ten years of seniority to take formal dependence, and for one who has ten years of seniority to give formal dependence.
And furthermore, monks, a teacher is to be taken up in this way:
having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet, having sat down in the kneeling position with the hands joined in reverential salutation, he should speak thus to him:"
“Venerable sir, be my teacher; depending on you, venerable sir, I shall go forth.
Venerable sir, be my teacher; depending on you, venerable sir, I shall go forth.
Venerable sir, be my teacher; depending on you, venerable sir, I shall go forth.”

If one makes a request by means of the body—saying “It is good,” or “It is easy,” or “It is appropriate,” or “It is suitable,” or “Please accomplish it in a pleasing manner”—or makes a request by means of speech, or makes a request by means of both body and speech, then the teacher is accepted.
If one does not make a request by means of the body, nor by means of speech, nor by means of both body and speech, then the teacher is not accepted.
Monks, a pupil must conduct himself properly toward his teacher.
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
having risen early, removing one's sandals, and arranging the upper robe over one shoulder, one should provide a tooth-stick, provide water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat.
If there is conjey, one should wash the vessel and bring the conjey forward.
After giving water to one who has drunk the gruel, he should receive the vessel, hold it low, wash it carefully without scraping it, and put it away.
When the teacher has risen, the seat should be removed.
If that place is dirty, that place should be swept.

If the teacher wishes to enter a village, the inner robe should be given to him; the outer robe should be received back; the waistband should be given; the upper robes should be given after folding them over; and the bowl, having been washed and rinsed, should be given.

If the teacher desires an attendant monk, [the student] should dress himself properly, covering the three circles, fasten the waistband, put on the upper robes after folding them over, and fasten the toggle.
Having washed the bowl and taken it, one should act as the attendant monk behind the teacher.
One should not go too far away, nor too close; one should receive whatever is placed into the bowl.
While the teacher is speaking, one should not interject with talk in between.
If the teacher speaks while approaching the vicinity of an offense, he should be stopped.
Upon his return, one should arrive first and prepare a seat; a foot-stool, a foot-stand, and a foot-washing stone should be set out;
one should go forward to meet him and receive his bowl and robe; and a spare lower garment should be given to him.
The lower robe should be accepted.
If the robe is damp, it should be dried in the sun for a short while, but the robe must not be left in the sun.
The robe should be folded.
When folding a robe, one should fold it with a four-finger width border left at the edge so that there is no breakage in the middle;
the waistband should be placed on the outer fold.
If there is almsfood and the teacher wishes to eat, one should give water and present the almsfood.
The teacher should be asked for water.

When he has finished eating, one should give him water, receive his bowl, hold it low, wash it carefully without scratching it, dry it, and let it dry for a short while in the heat; however, the bowl must not be left out in the heat.
The bowl and robes must be set aside.
When setting aside the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, touch the area beneath the bed or beneath the seat, and then set the bowl down.
The bowl must not be set down on the bare ground.

When putting away the robe-cloths, one should take hold of the cloth with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward oneself and the body toward the outside, and then put it away.
When the teacher has risen, the seat should be removed; the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-scraper should be put away.
If that place is dirty, it should be swept.
If the teacher wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared.
If he needs cold water, cold water should be prepared;
if he needs warm water, warm water should be prepared.
If the teacher wishes to enter the sauna, the powder should be kneaded, the clay moistened, and the sauna bench taken and followed behind the teacher.
Having entered, one should offer the sauna bench, receive the robe, and lay it aside to one side. Then the powder should be given and the clay should be given.
If one has the strength, one may enter the sauna.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover the front and back, and then enter.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior monks.
New monks should not be preempted from their seats.
In the sauna, service should be performed for the teacher.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench, cover it both in front and behind, and then exit the sauna.
Service should also be performed for the teacher in the water.
Having bathed first, emerged from the water, dried one's own limbs, and dressed oneself,
one should wipe the water from the teacher’s body, give him his lower robe, give him his upper robe, and [prepare] the sauna bench.
Having taken [the requisites] first, he should return and prepare a seat; he should set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone.
The teacher should be asked for drinking water.
If he wishes to have [the text] recited, it should be recited for him.
If he wishes to ask questions, he should ask them.
If the dwelling where the teacher resides is dirty, he should clean it if he is able.
When cleaning the dwelling, he should first take out his bowl and robe and set them aside.
Having taken out the sitting mat and rug, they should be placed to one side.
Having taken out the mattress and pillow, they should be placed to one side.
Having lowered the bed, one should take it out and place it to one side, doing so carefully without scraping it or knocking against the door frame.
Having lowered the seat so that it is not struck or brushed against, and without knocking against the surface of the door-panel, one should take it out and place it to one side.
Having taken out the bed-legs, they should be placed to one side.
Having taken out the spittoon, it should be placed to one side.
Having removed the back-slab, it should be set aside to one side.
Having observed the floor-covering as it was laid out, it should be removed and set aside to one side.
If there is mold in the dwelling, the ceiling should first be cleared, and the light-shafts, corners, and edges should be wiped clean.
If a wall treated with red ocher becomes stained, it should be wiped clean after moistening and squeezing out a cloth.
If a floor treated with black pigment becomes stained, it should be wiped clean after moistening and squeezing out a cloth.
If the floor is untreated, it should be sprinkled with water and then swept.
"Lest the monastery be defiled by dust.
Having sifted out the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
The floor-covering should be aired, cleaned, beaten, brought back inside, and spread out as it was previously arranged.
The bedstead supports and foot-rests, having been dried in the sun, wiped clean, and brought back, should be placed in their proper positions.
The bed, having been dried in the sun, cleaned, dusted, lowered, and carefully carried back without scratching it or knocking against the door frame, should be arranged as previously designated.
The chair, having been dried in the sun, cleaned, dusted, lowered, and carefully carried back without scratching it or knocking against the door frame, should be arranged as previously designated.
Having aired out the mattress and pillow, cleaned them, and shaken them out, one should bring them back and spread them out as they were originally arranged.
Having aired out the sitting rug, cleaned it, and shaken it out, one should bring it back and spread it out as it was originally arranged.
Having aired out the spittoon, wiped it clean, and brought it back, one should place it in its proper position.
Having dried the leaning board, wiped it, and brought it back, it should be placed in its proper place.
The bowl and robe should be set down.
When setting down the bowl, one should hold the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, touch the lower part of the bed or the lower part of the chair before setting the bowl down.
Furthermore, the robe must not be placed on ground that has not been cleared.

When putting away a robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, and then place the robe away.
If dusty winds are blowing from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the west, the western windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the north, the northern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the south, the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold weather, the windows should be opened during the day and closed at night.
If it is hot weather, the windows should be closed during the day and opened at night.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse must be swept.
If the assembly hall is dirty, the assembly hall must be swept.
If the fire-hall is dirty, the fire-hall must be swept.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If drinking water is not available, drinking water should be provided.
If washing water is not available, washing water should be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water should be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.
If dissatisfaction arises in the teacher, the pupil should dispel it himself, have it dispelled by another, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If remorse arises in the teacher, the pupil should dispel it himself, have it dispelled by another, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If a wrong view arises in the teacher, the pupil must resolve it, have it resolved, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If the teacher has committed a grave offense and deserves probation, the pupil must make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha grant probation to my teacher?"
If the teacher is deserving of being sent back to the beginning, the pupil should make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha send the teacher back to the beginning?
If the teacher is deserving of the *mānatta* discipline, the pupil should make an effort...
"How might the Saṅgha grant the *mānatta* penance to the teacher?
If the teacher is worthy of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), the pupil must make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha rehabilitate the teacher?"
If the Saṅgha intends to perform a formal act against the teacher—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the pupil should make an effort, thinking:
"How can the Saṅgha refrain from performing this act against my teacher, or how might it modify it to something lighter?

Furthermore, once the Saṅgha has performed such an act against him—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the pupil should make an effort [to assist his teacher].
"How might the teacher conduct himself properly, behave with humility, and act so as to bring this legal matter to an end, such that the Saṅgha would settle the case?
If the teacher's robe needs washing, the pupil should wash it, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How might the teacher's robe be washed?"
If a robe must be made for the teacher, the pupil should make it or make an effort,
thinking, "How can a robe be made for my teacher?
If dye must be boiled for the teacher, the pupil should boil it or make an effort.
"How indeed might the teacher’s dye be prepared?
If the teacher’s robe needs dyeing, the pupil must either dye it himself or make an effort, thinking:
"How indeed might the teacher’s robe be dyed?"
While dyeing a robe, one should dye it by turning it over thoroughly and repeatedly; one must not depart while the drops of dye have not yet dried.
Without having asked permission from one's teacher, one must not give a bowl to anyone, nor receive a bowl from anyone;
one must not give a robe to anyone.
One should not accept a robe from one person;
one should not give requisites to another;
nor should one accept requisites from another.
One should not have one person's hair cut;
one should not have another person's hair cut;
one should not perform services for another.
One should not have work performed by one person;
one should not perform services for another;
one should not have services performed by another.
One should not act as the attendant for another;
one should not accept another as one's attendant;
and one should not have almsfood brought out for another.
Almsfood must not be caused to be brought out by anyone alone.
One must not enter a village without having asked permission from one’s teacher; one must not go to a cemetery; one must not depart for another region.
If the teacher is ill, he must be attended to for as long as life lasts, and one must wait for his recovery.
The duties toward the teacher are finished.
19. Discussion of the Duties Toward the Pupil:
"Monks, the teacher should behave properly toward the pupil."
In this regard, this is the proper conduct:
Monks, a pupil should be supported and assisted by his teacher through recitation, questioning, exhortation, and instruction.
If the teacher has a bowl but the pupil does not have one, the teacher should give his bowl to the pupil, or he should make an effort to procure one for him.
"How might an alms bowl arise for the resident pupil?
If the teacher has a robe but the resident pupil does not have a robe, the teacher should give a robe to the resident pupil, or he should make an effort, thinking:
"How might a robe arise for the resident pupil?"
If the teacher has requisites but the pupil has none, the teacher should give the pupil his requisites or make an effort, thinking:
"How can requisites be obtained for the pupil?
If the pupil is ill, the teacher should rise early and give him a tooth-stick, water for rinsing the mouth, and prepare a seat.
If there is rice gruel, he should wash the vessel and offer the gruel.
After the pupil has drunk the gruel, he should give him water, receive the vessel, hold it low, and wash it carefully without clashing it against anything, then set it aside.
When the pupil has risen, the seat should be removed.
If that place is dirty, that place should be swept.

If the student wishes to enter the village, the inner robe should be given to him, the outer robe received back, the waistband should be given, the upper robes should be given to him after folding them over [the shoulder], and the bowl should be given to him after washing it and rinsing it with water.
Thinking, "He will return at this time," a seat should be prepared, along with water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone.
It should be set down; one should go out to meet them and receive their bowl and robe;
a lower garment should be given to them, and their lower garment should be received.
If the robe is damp, it should be dried in the sun for a short while, but the robe must not be left in the sun.
The robe should be folded.
When folding the robe, one should fold it after turning back the edge by four finger-breadths,
so that there is no tearing in the middle.
The waistband should be put on.
If there is almsfood and the resident pupil wishes to eat, one should give him water and offer the almsfood.
The resident pupil should be asked for drinking water.

Having given water to one who has finished eating, and having taken the bowl, having lowered it, and having washed it carefully without scratching it, and having removed the remaining water, it should be dried for a short while in the warmth; however, the bowl must not be placed directly in the heat.
The bowl and robe should be put away.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand and, with the other hand, touch the lower part of the bed or the lower part of the chair before setting the bowl down.
Furthermore, the bowl should not be placed on ground that has not been cleared.

When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the far side and the fold toward the near side, and then put away the robe.
Once the pupil has left, the seat should be removed, and the water for washing the feet, the footstool, and the foot-wiping cloth should be put away.
If that place is dirty, that place should be swept.
If the resident pupil wishes to bathe, the bath should be prepared.
If there is need for cold water, cold water should be prepared.
If there is need for heat, heat should be prepared.
If the resident pupil wishes to enter the sauna, the powder should be kneaded, the clay moistened,
and having taken the sauna-bench, one should go and set out the sauna-bench, receive his robe, and [place it] to one side.
The seat should be set aside, powder should be given, and clay should be given.
If one is able, one should enter the sauna.
When entering the sauna, one should smear the face with clay, cover both the front and the back, and then enter the sauna.
One should not sit encroaching upon the senior bhikkhus, nor should one block junior bhikkhus from their seats.
In the sauna, one should perform service for one’s pupil.
When leaving the sauna, one should take the sauna-bench and exit the sauna after covering oneself both in front and behind.
Service should also be performed for the resident pupil even while in the water.
Having bathed first, emerged from the water, dried one’s own limbs, and put on one’s undergarment,
