one should wipe the water from the resident pupil’s body, give him his undergarment, give him his upper robe, and [prepare] the sauna bench.
Having taken [the requisites], he should return first and prepare a seat; he should set out water for washing the feet, a footstool, and a foot-washing stone.
The student should be asked if he needs drinking water.
If the dwelling where the student resides is dirty, it should be cleaned if he is able to do so.
While cleaning the dwelling, one should first take out the bowl and robes and set them aside;
having taken out the sitting mat and the sheet, they should be set aside;
having taken out the mattress and the pillow, they should be set aside.
Having lowered the bed, one should carry it out and set it aside to one side, taking care not to strike it or to let it brush against the door frame;
having lowered the chair, one should carry it out and set it aside to one side, taking care not to strike it or to let it brush against the door frame;
the bedstead supports should also be carried out and set aside to one side.
The spittoon should be removed and placed to one side;
the leaning board should be removed and placed to one side;
and the floor-covering, having noted where it was laid out, should be removed and placed to one side.
If there is mold on the dwelling, it should first be removed from the ceiling; the openings for light and the corners should be wiped clean.
If a wall treated with red ochre has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the floor treated with black pigment has become moldy, a cloth should be moistened, wrung out, and used to wipe it clean.
If the ground has not been prepared, it should be sprinkled with water and swept, thinking:
"Lest the dwelling be covered in dust.
Having cleared away the refuse, it should be discarded to one side.
Having dried, cleaned, and beaten out the ground-covering, he should bring it back and spread it out as it was previously arranged.
Having dried and wiped the bed-legs, he should bring them back and place them in their proper positions.

Having dried, cleaned, and beaten out the bed, he should lower it and, being very careful not to scratch it and not to strike the door-panel, he should bring it back and spread it out as it was previously arranged.

Having aired out the bed, cleaned it, and dusted it, having lowered it, one should bring it back and arrange it as designated, carefully without scraping it or knocking it against the surface of the door.
Having aired out the mattress and pillow, cleaned them, and dusted them, one should bring them back and arrange them as designated.
Having aired out the sitting mat and rug, cleaned them, and dusted them, one should bring them back and arrange them as designated.
The spittoon, having been dried, wiped, and brought back, should be placed in its proper place.
The leaning-board, having been dried, wiped, and brought back, should be placed in its proper place.
The bowl and robes should be put away.
When putting away the bowl, one should take hold of the bowl with one hand, touch the base of the bed or the base of the chair with the other hand, and then set down the bowl.
The bowl must not be set down on the bare ground.

When putting away the robe, one should take hold of the robe with one hand, wipe the robe-stand or the robe-string with the other hand, fold the edge toward the outside and the fold toward the inside, and then set down the robe.
If dusty winds blow from the east, the eastern windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the west, the western windows should be closed.
If dusty winds blow from the north, the northern windows should be closed.
If the winds blow from the south, the southern windows should be closed.
If it is cold, the windows should be opened by day and closed at night.
If it is hot, the windows should be closed by day and opened at night.
If the courtyard is dirty, the courtyard should be swept.
If the storehouse is dirty, the storehouse should be swept.
If the assembly hall is dirty, the assembly hall should be swept.
If the fire-hall is dirty, the fire-hall should be swept.
If the restroom is dirty, the restroom should be swept.
If there is no drinking water, drinking water should be provided.
If there is no food for consumption, food for consumption should be provided.
If there is no water in the rinsing-pitcher, water should be poured into the rinsing-pitcher.
If dissatisfaction has arisen in the resident pupil, the teacher should dispel it himself, have it dispelled by another, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If remorse arises in a pupil, the teacher should dispel it, have it dispelled, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If a wrong view arises in a pupil, the teacher should separate him from it, have him separated from it, or give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
If a pupil has committed a heavy offense and deserves probation, the teacher should make an effort [to help him].
"How might the Sangha grant probation to the pupil?
If the pupil is deserving of being sent back to the beginning, the teacher should make an effort:
"How might the Sangha send the pupil back to the beginning?"
If the pupil is deserving of the *mānatta* penance, the teacher must make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha grant the *mānatta* penance to my pupil?
If the pupil is deserving of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*), the teacher must make an effort [thinking the same].
"How might the Saṅgha rehabilitate the pupil?
If the Saṅgha intends to perform a formal act against the pupil—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the teacher must make an effort, thinking:
"How might the Saṅgha not carry out the formal act against the pupil, or how might it modify it to something lighter?"

Furthermore, if a formal act has been carried out against him by the Saṅgha—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension—the teacher should make an effort, thinking:
"How can my pupil behave properly, show respect, conduct himself so as to deserve release, and cause the Saṅgha to rescind that formal act?
If the pupil’s robe needs washing, the teacher should instruct him: "You should wash it in this manner."
Or he should make an effort, thinking: "How can the pupil's robe be washed?
If the pupil's robe needs to be made, the teacher should instruct him: "Make it like this," or he should make an effort, thinking: "How can the pupil's robe be made?"
If the student has dye to boil, the teacher should instruct him,
"Boil it in this way," or he should make an effort, thinking, "How can the student's dye be boiled?
If the student has a robe to dye, the teacher should instruct him, "Dye it in this way."
Or one should make an effort, thinking: "How can I have the student's robe dyed?
When dyeing the robe, it should be turned over carefully and dyed repeatedly; one must not leave while the drops of dye are still dripping.
If the student is ill, he should be attended to for as long as life lasts, and one should wait for his recovery.
The Duties of a Resident Disciple are finished.

20. Requesting Permission to Depart.
Now at that time, the pupils did not behave properly toward their teachers...
[they] reported this matter to the Blessed One...
"Monks, a pupil must not fail to behave properly toward his teacher."
“Whoever does not conduct themselves properly commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Yet they did not conduct themselves properly.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] …
“I allow you, monks, to dismiss one who does not behave properly.
And how, monks, should he be dismissed? One may say:
‘I dismiss you,’ or ‘Do not return here,’ or ‘Take away your bowl and robe,’ or ‘I am not to be attended by you.’”
“If one makes it known by body, makes it known by speech, or makes it known by both body and speech, the pupil is dismissed;
if one does not make it known by body, does not make it known by speech, and does not make it known by both body and speech, the pupil is not dismissed.
Now at that time, pupils who had been dismissed did not ask for forgiveness.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to ask for forgiveness,” he said.
Yet they still did not ask for forgiveness.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who has been dismissed should not fail to ask for forgiveness.
Whoever does not ask for forgiveness commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, teachers being asked for forgiveness would not forgive.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to forgive,” he said.
They did not tolerate it.
The resident pupils departed, left the order, or even went over to other sects.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who is asked for forgiveness must forgive.
Whoever does not forgive commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, teachers were dismissing those who were conducting themselves properly, yet they were not dismissing those who were conducting themselves improperly.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who is conducting himself correctly should not be dismissed.
Whoever should dismiss him commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
"And, monks, one who does not behave properly must not be dismissed.
Whoever does not dismiss him commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, a pupil endowed with five qualities may be dismissed."
"If a student lacks excessive affection for the teacher, lacks excessive confidence, lacks excessive moral shame, lacks excessive reverence, and lacks excessive cultivation [of the teachings]—
endowed with these five factors, monks, a student should be dismissed.
Endowed with five factors, monks, a student should not be dismissed."

“Bhikkhus, a pupil who possesses these five qualities should not be dismissed: he has excessive affection for his teacher, excessive confidence in him, excessive moral shame, excessive reverence for him, and excessive devotion to him.
Bhikkhus, a pupil who possesses these five qualities is fit to be dismissed.”

“Bhikkhus, when a pupil possesses five qualities, he is fit to be dismissed: he has no excessive affection for his teacher, no excessive confidence in him, no excessive sense of shame before him, no excessive respect for him, and no excessive devotion toward him.
Possessing these five qualities, bhikkhus, a pupil is fit to be dismissed.
But when a pupil possesses five [other] qualities, bhikkhus, he is not fit to be dismissed.”

“Bhikkhus, when a pupil possesses five qualities, he is not fit to be dismissed by his teacher: he has excessive affection for the teacher, excessive confidence in him, excessive moral shame, excessive reverence for him, and excessive devotion to him.
Bhikkhus, if a teacher does not dismiss a pupil who possesses these five qualities, he commits an offense; if he dismisses such a pupil, he is without offense.”

“Bhikkhus, when a student possesses these five factors—excessive love for the teacher, excessive confidence in him, excessive moral shame before him, excessive reverence for him, and excessive devotion to his development—the teacher who does not dismiss such a student commits an offense;

dismissing him, however, is not an offense. Bhikkhus, when a student possesses these five factors—lack of excessive love for the teacher, lack of excessive confidence in him, lack of excessive moral shame before him, lack of excessive reverence for him, and lack of excessive devotion to his development—the teacher who dismisses such a student commits an offense; not dismissing him, however, is not an offense.”
“Bhikkhus, there is excessive affection for the teacher, excessive confidence in him, excessive moral shame, excessive reverence for him, and excessive devotion to him.
Bhikkhus, when a teacher dismisses a pupil who possesses these five qualities, he is at fault; when he does not dismiss him, he is not at fault.
The section on dismissal and reconciliation is finished.
21. The Story of the Foolish and Incompetent [Monks] Now at that time, monks who were foolish and incompetent, thinking "I have ten years," "I have ten years," gave formal dependence (*nissaya*).
It was seen that the teachers were foolish while the resident pupils were wise.
Invisible are teachers who are incompetent while their pupils are competent;
invisible are teachers who are of little learning while their pupils are very learned;
invisible are teachers who are lacking in wisdom while their pupils are wise.
Those bhikkhus who were few in desires... they complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these foolish and incompetent bhikkhus grant formal dependence [nissaya], thinking, 'We have ten years of seniority; we have ten years of seniority'?
It is seen that there are foolish teachers with wise pupils; it is seen that there are incompetent teachers with competent pupils."
“Teachers are seen who have little learning while their pupils are very learned; teachers are seen who lack wisdom while their pupils are wise.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One … [as before] … “Is it true, bhikkhus, that the bhikkhus say this?”
“‘Ten years, ten years’—
thus fools and the incompetent give dependence...
‘It is true, Blessed One.’”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him...
having rebuked him...
and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, support should not be given by one who is ignorant and incompetent.
Whoever should give it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, I allow support to be given by a monk who is competent, capable, and has ten years of seniority or more.”

Sitting to one side, Suddhodana the Sakyan said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, I would ask a boon of the Blessed One.
"The Tathāgatas, Gotama, have transcended boons," [the Blessed One replied].
“Whatever, venerable sir, is allowable and whatever is blameless.
“Speak, Gotama,” [the Blessed One said].
“When the Blessed One went forth, venerable sir, there was no small suffering for me; likewise for Nanda, and it was even more excessive for Rāhula.”
"Venerable sir, love for one's children cuts through the outer skin; having cut through the outer skin, it cuts through the inner skin; having cut through the inner skin, it cuts through the flesh;
having cut through the flesh, it cuts through the sinews; having cut through the sinews, it cuts through the bone;
and having cut through the bone, it remains having reached the marrow."
"It would be well, venerable sir, if the masters would not ordain a son without the permission of his parents.
Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened Suddhodana the Sakyan with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, Suddhodana the Sakyan rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and departed.
Then the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with regard to this cause and this occasion, addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, a son must not be ordained without the permission of his mother and father.
Whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Kapilavatthu for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Sāvatthī.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a family who were supporters of the Venerable Sāriputta sent a young boy to the presence of the Venerable Sāriputta,
saying, "May the Elder ordain this boy.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“The Blessed One has laid down the rule:
‘One should not have two novices attend upon oneself.
And this novice Rāhula is mine.”
“What indeed should I do?
He reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a learned and competent monk to have two novices attend upon him; or as many as he is able to exhort and instruct.”
42. Discussion on the Training Rules (Sikkhāpada-kathā).
Then it occurred to the novices:
"How many training rules do we have, and where must we train?"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One...
[as before] ... “Monks, I allow ten training rules for novices, and that novices should train in them:
abstention from taking life;”
Abstaining from taking what is not given,
abstaining from unchastity,
and abstaining from false speech.
Abstaining from fermented and distilled liquors, intoxicants, and substances causing heedlessness;
abstaining from eating at improper times;
and abstaining from dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the viewing of frivolous spectacles.
Abstaining from wearing garlands, using scents and unguents, and adorning or beautifying oneself;
abstaining from high and luxurious beds and seats;
and abstaining from accepting gold and silver.
“I allow, monks, these ten training rules for novices, and that novices train in them. Now at that time,
the novices lived without respect for the monks, without deference, and did not conduct themselves in a manner befitting them.
The bhikkhus were indignant, disparaged [them], and complained, saying:
"How can these novices live among the bhikkhus without respect, without deference, and without conduct befitting them?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before]...
“Monks, I allow you to carry out disciplinary action against a novice who possesses five qualities:

he strives for the non-gain of the monks; he strives for the harm of the monks; [he strives for the non-fame of the monks; he strives for the ill-repute of the monks; he speaks in dispraise of the monks].”
He strives for the non-residence of monks;
he reviles and abuses monks;
he causes monks to be divided from other monks.
“I allow you, monks, to carry out disciplinary action against a novice who is possessed of these five qualities.
Then it occurred to the monks,
“What kind of disciplinary action should be carried out?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to set up a restriction,” he said.
Now at that time, monks were setting up restrictions for novices across the entire monastery grounds.
Unable to enter the monastery, the novices would depart, disrobe, or even go over to the sectarians.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, not the entire monastery grounds should be closed off.”
Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
"I allow you, monks, to place a restriction on whatever place one dwells in or from which one returns.
Now at that time, the monks placed a restriction on the food that was to be taken directly by the mouth of the novices.
When people were providing rice porridge or meals for the Saṅgha, they would say to the novices,
“Come, venerable sirs, drink the rice porridge;
come, venerable sirs, eat the meal.”
The novices said this:
“It is not possible, friends;
the bhikkhus have placed an obstruction.”
People criticized, grumbled, and complained,
saying, “How can the venerable ones place an obstacle to the food that enters the mouth of the novices?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not place an obstacle in the way of food brought to the door of the mouth.
Whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The section on disciplinary action is finished.
44. The Account of Obstructing Without Permission.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were obstructing novices without having asked their preceptors for permission.
The preceptors went searching for them.
“How is it that our novice monks are not to be seen?
The monks said,
“Friends, an obstruction has been placed by the group of six monks.”
The preceptors complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks, without asking us for permission, place restrictions on our novices?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one must not impose a restriction without having asked the preceptor.
Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing.
45. The Matter of Dissuading.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were harassing the novices of the elder monks.
The elders grew weary, having to fetch tooth-sticks and mouth-watering water themselves.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not incite another’s assembly.
Whoever should so incite it, there is an offense of wrong-doing. 46.

They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to expel a novice who possesses ten qualities.

He takes what is not given,

The bhikkhus were repelled.

“Come, friends, defile me.
The elephant trainers and horse trainers defiled him.

“These ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, are eunuchs.
Even those among them who are not eunuchs defile these eunuchs.
Thus, they are all unchaste.”
The monks heard those elephant-trainers and horse-trainers complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one who is a paṇḍaka, if not yet ordained, should not be ordained; if already ordained, he should be expelled.”
48. The Case of One Living in Communion through Theft Now at that time, there was a certain son of an ancient noble family whose lineage had declined, who was very delicate.
Then this thought occurred to that son of an ancient noble family whose lineage had declined:
“I am indeed delicate; I am not capable of acquiring wealth not yet acquired, nor of increasing wealth already acquired.
By what means might I live in comfort and not come to exhaustion?
Then it occurred to that former gentleman of exhausted lineage:
“These recluses, sons of the Sakyans, are easy in their virtue and easy in their conduct; having eaten fine food, they lie down on beds sheltered from the wind.
What if I were to prepare my own bowl and robes, shave off my hair and beard, put on saffron-colored garments, go to the monastery, and live together with the bhikkhus?

Then that man of ancient family, of exhausted lineage, prepared his own bowl and robes, shaved off his hair and beard, put on saffron-colored garments, went to the monastery, and paid homage to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus said this:
“How many years of seniority do you have, friend?
“What is this, friends? What does ‘how many years of seniority’ mean?”
“But who, friend, is your preceptor?
“What is this, friend, that you call a ‘preceptor’?
The bhikkhus said this to the Venerable Upāli:
“Come now, friend Upāli, you must question this renunciant.
Then that son of an ancient noble family, whose lineage was exhausted, being questioned by the Venerable Upāli, reported this matter.
The Venerable Upāli reported this matter to the monks.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one who lives in communion by theft, if unordained, is not to be ordained; if already ordained, he is to be expelled.
Monks, one who has gone over to another sect, if unordained, is not to be ordained; if already ordained, he is to be expelled.”
49. The Story of the Animal Realm.
Now at that time, a certain nāga was distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by his birth in the nāga realm.
Then this thought occurred to that nāga:
“By what means indeed might I be released from this birth as a nāga and quickly regain human status?
Then it occurred to that nāga:
“These ascetics, followers of the Sakyan son, are practitioners of the Dhamma, practitioners of equanimity, practitioners of the holy life, speakers of truth, virtuous, and of noble character.”
“If I were to go forth among the ascetics who are followers of the Sakyan son, then I would be released from this naga-birth and would quickly regain human status.
Thereupon, that naga approached the monks in the form of a young brahmin and requested the going-forth.
The monks granted him the going-forth and conferred full ordination upon him.
Now at that time, that nāga was staying in a certain frontier monastery together with a certain bhikkhu.
Then, as the night was drawing toward dawn, that bhikkhu rose and was walking back and forth in the open air.
When the bhikkhu had gone out, the nāga let his guard down and fell asleep.
The entire dwelling was filled with snakes, and their coils were protruding from the windows.

Then, as that bhikkhu was pushing open the door, thinking, "I shall enter the dwelling," he saw the entire dwelling filled with snakes and their coils protruding from the windows. Seeing this, he cried out in terror.
The bhikkhus ran up to him and said this to him:
“Friend, why did you let out that cry?
“Friend, this entire monastery is full of snakes; their coils have come out through the windows.
Then that nāga, awakened by that sound, sat down upon his own seat.
The bhikkhus asked,
“Who are you, friend?
“I am a nāga, venerable sirs,” he replied.
“But why, friend, did you do such a thing?
Then that nāga explained the matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported the matter to the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having assembled the community of monks, said this to that nāga:
“Indeed, you nāgas are incapable of growth in this Dhamma and Discipline.

Go, nāga, right there observe the Uposatha on the fourteenth, the fifteenth, and the eighth day of the fortnight; in this way you will be released from the nāga womb and will quickly regain human status.”
Then that nāga, being incapable of growth, thinking, "Alas, in this Dhamma and Vinaya," became sorrowful and dejected; shedding tears and letting out a cry, he departed.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, there are these two conditions for a nāga to reveal his true nature."
And when he engages in sexual intercourse with his own kind, and when, being unrestrained, he falls asleep—these, monks, are the two conditions for a nāga to manifest his true nature.
A nāga who is a mere animal, monks, should not be ordained if unordained; if already ordained, he should be expelled.”

52. The Story of the Killer of an Arahant Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were traveling on the highway from Sāketa to Sāvatthī.
On the way, some bandits came out, robbed some of the bhikkhus, and killed others.
The king’s officers of Sāvatthī set out and captured some of the bandits, while others of the bandits fled.
Those who had fled went forth among the monks, whereas those who were captured were being led away for execution.
Those who had fled and gone forth saw the bandits being led away for execution; having seen them, they said this:
“It was well indeed that we fled; for if we had been captured, we too would have been slain in just this way.
The monks asked them, “But what did you do, friends?”
Then those renunciants reported this matter to the monks.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“These monks, bhikkhus, are arahants.”
“Monks, one who has killed an arahant, if not yet ordained, must not be ordained; if already ordained, he must be expelled.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhunīs were traveling on the road from Sāketa to Sāvatthī.
On the way, bandits emerged and robbed some of the bhikkhunīs, while they violated others.
From Sāvatthī, the king’s men emerged and captured some of the bandits, while other bandits fled.
Those who fled went forth among the bhikkhus.
Those who were captured were led away for execution.
Those who had fled and gone forth into homelessness saw those bandits being led away for execution, and seeing them, they said:
"It is well indeed that we have fled; for if we had been captured, we too would have been executed in just this same way."
The bhikkhus said,
"But what, friends, have you done?
Then those wanderers informed the bhikkhus of this matter.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, one who has raped a bhikkhunī, if unordained, is not to be ordained; if already ordained, he is to be expelled.

Now at that time, monks were granting full ordination with the Saṅgha as the preceptor.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

They reported this matter to the Blessed One:

“Monks, one who does not possess a bowl must not be ordained.
Whoever should ordain him commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, monks were ordaining those who did not possess a robe.
They wander for alms naked.
People grumble, complain, and spread it about,
saying, "They are just like the heretics."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who lacks a robe should not be ordained.
Whoever should ordain him, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, monks were giving full ordination to those who had neither bowls nor robes.
They went about for alms with their hands bare.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“Just like the sectarians,” they reported this matter to the Blessed One. “Monks,
one who does not possess a bowl and robes must not be ordained.”
"Whoever should confer full ordination [with such a bowl], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the monks conferred full ordination with a borrowed bowl;
once the person was ordained, they returned the bowl.
They wandered for alms with their hands [empty].
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about,
saying, "They are just like the heretics."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not confer full ordination using a borrowed bowl.
Whoever should confer it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the monks were conferring full ordination using borrowed robes.
Once the person was ordained, they returned the robes;
consequently, they went for alms naked.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained,
saying, “They are just like the sectarians.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not confer full ordination with borrowed robes.
Whoever should confer it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, monks were conferring full ordination with borrowed bowls and robes.
When they had been ordained, they were presented with bowls and robes;
yet they wandered for alms naked with their hands held out.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“It is just like the sectarians.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not grant full ordination using borrowed bowl and robes.”
Whoever should confer full ordination, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
The section on those not to be fully ordained consisting of twenty-one cases is finished.

Now at that time, monks were giving the going-forth to those with severed hands...
[and so on] ...to those with severed feet...
[and so on] ...to those with severed hands and feet... [and so on].

They grant the going forth to one whose finger has been severed …pe… they grant the going forth to one whose ankle has been severed …pe… they grant the going forth to one whose Achilles tendon has been severed …pe…
They give the going-forth to one with a hand like a snake’s hood …pe… they give the going-forth to a hunchback …pe… they give the going-forth to a dwarf …pe…
They give the going-forth to one with a goitre...
[and so on] ...they give the going-forth to one branded with a mark...
[and so on] ...they give the going-forth to one whipped with a lash... [and so on].
They give the going-forth to those who have committed a written offense...
they give the going-forth to those with a foot deformity... they give the going-forth to those suffering from a foul disease... [and so on]... they give the going-forth to those who are criminals.
They give the going-forth to one who corrupts the assembly …pe… they give the going-forth to one who is blind in one eye …pe… they give the going-forth to one who has a withered arm …pe…
They give the going-forth to one who is lame …pe… they give the going-forth to one whose wings are broken …pe… they give the going-forth to one whose modes of deportment are impaired …pe…
They give the going-forth to one weakened by old age...
they give the going-forth to a blind person...
they give the going-forth to a mute person... [and so forth].
They give the going-forth to one who is deaf …pe… they give the going-forth to one who is blind and mute …pe… they give the going-forth to one who is both blind and deaf …pe…
They give the going-forth to those who are mute and deaf...
[and so on] ...they give the going-forth to those who are blind, mute, and deaf.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so on].
“Monks, one whose hand has been cut off should not be ordained …pe… monks,
one whose foot has been cut off should not be ordained …pe… monks,
one whose hands and feet have been cut off should not be ordained …pe…”
“Monks, one who has had his ears cut off should not be given the going forth...
Monks, one who has had his nose cut off should not be given the going forth...
Monks, one who has had both his ears and nose cut off should not be given the going forth...”
“Monks, one with severed fingers should not be given the going-forth …pe… monks,
one with severed heels should not be given the going-forth …pe… monks,
one with severed tendons should not be given the going-forth …pe…”
“Monks, one with webbed hands should not be ordained …pe… monks,
a hunchback should not be ordained …pe… monks,
a dwarf should not be ordained …pe…”
“Monks, one with a goiter should not be given the going-forth …pe… monks,
one struck by a mark should not be given the going-forth …pe… monks,
one struck by a whip should not be given the going-forth …pe…”

one with elephantiasis should not be given the going-forth …pe… monks,
one afflicted by a foul disease should not be given the going-forth …pe…”
“Monks, one who corrupts the assembly should not be given the going-forth …pe… monks,
one who is blind in one eye should not be given the going-forth …pe… monks,
one who has a crooked limb should not be given the going-forth …pe…”

Monks, one who has a withered arm should not be admitted into the order...

one who is blind should not be given the going-forth …pe… monks,

The section on the thirty-two cases of those not to be ordained is finished.
The ninth recitation-section, the Section on Inheritance, is finished.
58. The Matter of Dependence for the Shameless.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks gave formal support (*nissaya*) to shameless monks.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, formal support must not be given to shameless monks."
“Whoever should give [it], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, monks were living in dependence upon shameless persons;
before long, they too became shameless and evil.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not live in dependence on those who are shameless.
Whoever should so live, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Then it occurred to the bhikkhus:
"It has been laid down by the Blessed One:
'Support should not be given to those who are shameless, nor should one live in dependence on those who are shameless.'"
“How indeed may we know whether he is modest or shameless?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to wait for four or five days until I know his character as a monk.”
59. The Matter of Reliance for Those Travelling, etc.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was traveling along a highway in the Kosala country.
Then it occurred to that bhikkhu:
“The Blessed One has laid down:
‘One should not dwell without formal support.
Yet I am one who requires formal support and have set out on a long journey. How, indeed, should I proceed?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a monk who has set out on a journey and is unable to obtain formal dependence (nissaya) to live without dependence.
Now at that time, two monks were traveling along a highway in the Kosala country.
They arrived at a certain monastery.
There, one bhikkhu was ill. Then, this thought occurred to that sick bhikkhu:
“The Blessed One has prescribed:
‘One should not live without formal support.
Yet I am ill and require formal support; how, then, should I proceed?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a sick monk who cannot obtain formal support to live without support.
Then, it occurred to that monk who was attending to the sick one:
“The Blessed One has prescribed:
‘One should not live without formal support.
Yet I am one who requires formal support, and this bhikkhu is ill. How, then, should I proceed?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow a monk who is attending to the sick, if he is unable to obtain formal dependence (nissaya) and is being asked for it, to live without dependence (anissita).
Now at that time, a certain monk was dwelling in the forest.
And he found comfort in that lodging.
Then it occurred to that bhikkhu:
"It has been prescribed by the Blessed One—"
"One should not dwell without formal dependence.
"I am one who must take formal dependence, yet I am dwelling in the forest, and I find comfort in this lodging. How, indeed, should I proceed?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, for a forest-dwelling monk who is seeking a comfortable stay and who does not obtain formal dependence, to live without dependence [with the thought]:
‘When a suitable giver of dependence arrives, then I will live under his dependence.
60. The Allowance for Proclamation by Lineage.
Now at that time, there was one who desired to receive full ordination from the Venerable Mahākassapa.
Then the Venerable Mahākassapa sent a messenger to the presence of the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Let Ānanda come; let him perform the proclamation for this person."
The Venerable Ānanda spoke thus:
"I am not able to utter the name of the Elder; the Elder is venerable to me.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to announce [the candidate’s name] even by clan.
Now at that time, two persons seeking full ordination were present before the Venerable Mahākassapa.
They disputed with one another, saying, “I shall be the first to attain full ordination; I shall be the first to attain full ordination.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to perform two [ordinations] with a single proclamation.
Now at that time, several elders were desirous of receiving full ordination.
They fell into dispute:
“I shall be the first to receive full ordination; I shall be the first to receive full ordination!
The elders said, “Come now, friends, let us all perform the formal act of proclamation together.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to perform two or three formal proclamations; and that must be done with one preceptor, and not without a preceptor.
62. Allowance for Ordination of Those Conceived in the Womb.
Now at that time, the Venerable Kumārakassapa had been ordained for ten years since his conception.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Kumārakassapa:
“It has been laid down by the Blessed One:”
‘A person less than twenty years of age should not be ordained.
Now, I was ordained at twenty by counting the time spent in the womb. Am I truly ordained, or am I not ordained?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, that first thought which arose in the mother's womb, that first consciousness which appeared—starting from that, there is his birth.
Monks, I allow you to confer full ordination upon one who has been in the womb for twenty years."
63. The Procedure for Ordination.
Now at that time, those who had received full ordination were seen to be afflicted with leprosy, boils, ringworm, consumption, and epilepsy.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, when conferring full ordination, to ask about the thirteen obstructive conditions.
And furthermore, monks, he should be asked thus:
‘Do you have such diseases as these?’”
Are you free from leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, and epilepsy?
Are you a human being?
Are you a man?
Are you a free man?
Are you free from debt?
Are you not a royal servant?
Have you been permitted by your mother and father?
Are you twenty years of age?
Is your bowl and robe complete?
“What is your name?
What is the name of your preceptor?
At that time, however, the monks were questioning those seeking ordination about the obstructing factors even before they had been instructed.
Those seeking full ordination were embarrassed and abashed; they were unable to answer.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Monks, I allow you to first instruct them and afterwards question them regarding the obstructing conditions."
Right there in the midst of the Saṅgha they instructed them.
Those seeking full ordination stood there in a state of hesitation and became bashful; they were unable to answer.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, after having instructed [the candidate] in private, to question him concerning the obstructing factors in the midst of the Saṅgha.
And furthermore, monks, he should be instructed in this way:
first, he should be made to take a preceptor.”
Having had him take a preceptor, the bowl and robes should be pointed out to him:
“This is your bowl; this is your outer robe (saṅghāṭi); this is your upper robe (uttarāsaṅga);
this is your inner robe (antaravāsaka). Go and stand in that place.”
Immature and incompetent [monks] were giving instruction.
Those seeking ordination, being poorly instructed, became distressed and abashed; they were unable to answer.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one who is foolish and incompetent should not give instruction.
Whoever should so instruct, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow an experienced and competent monk to give instruction.”
Those who had not been appointed were giving instruction.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one who has not been appointed must not give instruction.”
Whoever should instruct [her] commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, for one who has been formally authorized to instruct.
And thus, monks, should she be authorized:
Either one may appoint oneself, or another may be appointed by another.
And how is one to appoint oneself?
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Sangha listen to me.
So-and-so desires the full ordination from the venerable so-and-so.
If it is agreeable to the Sangha, may I instruct so-and-so.’
In this way, one should appoint oneself.
But how should another be appointed by another?
A learned and competent monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me.
So-and-so desires the full ordination from the venerable So-and-so.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let So-and-so instruct So-and-so.’
In this way, one person is to be appointed by another.
The monk who has been so appointed, having approached the one seeking full ordination, should address him thus:
“Listen, [Name], this is the time for truth, the time for reality.”
When they ask about what has arisen in the midst of the Saṅgha, if it exists, one should say "it exists";
if it does not exist, one should say "it does not exist. Do not be prolix, and do not be dejected.
This is how they will question you.
Do you have such diseases as leprosy, boils, ringworm, consumption, or epilepsy?
Are you a human being?
Are you a man?
Are you a free man?
Are you free from debt?
Are you a royal servant?
Have you been permitted by your mother and father?
Are you twenty years of age?
“Is your bowl and robe complete?
What is your name?
What is the name of your preceptor?”
“They come together from one side.
‘Monks, you must not come together from one side.
The instructor, having arrived first, should inform the Saṅgha:’”
"Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
So-and-so desires the full ordination from the Venerable So-and-so.
He has been instructed by me."
"If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let such-and-such a person come.
He should be told, "Come.

Having had him arrange his upper robe over one shoulder, make him pay homage at the feet of the monks, have him sit in the kneeling position, and have him raise his joined palms, he should be made to request ordination:
“Venerable Sir, I request ordination from the Saṅgha.
May the Saṅgha, out of compassion, lift me up.
For a second time, Venerable Sir, I request ordination from the Saṅgha.”
‘Venerable sir, let the Saṅgha lift me up out of compassion.
For a third time, venerable sir, I request full ordination from the Saṅgha.
Venerable sir, let the Saṅgha lift me up out of compassion.’”
A competent monk who knows the procedure should inform the Sangha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me.
This person named so-and-so desires the full ordination from the Venerable named so-and-so.”
"If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, may I question [you], so-and-so, regarding the obstructing states?
Listen, so-and-so; this is your time for truth, your time for reality.
I ask you what has happened.
If it exists, it should be said to exist; if it does not exist, it should be said not to exist.
Do you have such ailments as leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, or epilepsy?
Are you a human being?
Are you a male?
Are you a free person?
Are you free from debt?
Are you not a royal servant?
Have you been permitted by your parents?
Are you twenty years of age?
Is your bowl and robe complete?
What is your name?
‘What is the name of your preceptor?
A competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha:
‘Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.’
This person named [Name], desiring full ordination from the Venerable [Name], is pure regarding the obstructing conditions and possesses his bowl and robes complete.
This person named [Name] requests full ordination from the Saṅgha with [Name] as preceptor.
If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant full ordination to this person named [Name] with [Name] as preceptor.
This is the motion.
Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me.
This person named so-and-so desires the full ordination from the Venerable so-and-so; he is pure regarding the obstructing conditions, and his bowl and robes are complete.
The one named so-and-so requests full ordination from the Sangha with so-and-so as preceptor.
The Sangha grants full ordination to so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor.
Whichever venerable one approves of the full ordination of so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve of this, let him speak.
For a second time, I state this matter:
Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs.
This person, named so-and-so, desires full ordination from the Venerable named so-and-so; he is pure regarding the obstructing conditions, and his bowl and robes are complete.
This person, named so-and-so, requests full ordination from the Sangha with so-and-so as preceptor.
The Sangha grants full ordination to this person, named so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor.
Whichever venerable one approves of the full ordination of [Name] with [Name] as preceptor, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
For the third time I state this matter:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This person named so-and-so desires full ordination from the venerable one named so-and-so; he is pure regarding the obstructing conditions, and his bowl and robes are complete.
So-and-so requests full ordination from the Saṅgha with so-and-so as preceptor."
The Saṅgha confers full ordination upon [name], with [name] as preceptor.
Whichever venerable one approves of the full ordination of [name] with [name] as preceptor, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“Such-and-such a person has been ordained by the Saṅgha with such-and-such a person as preceptor.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
The formal act of ordination is concluded.

64. The Four Supports: “At that very moment, the shadow must be measured; the measure of the season must be announced; the portion of the day must be announced; the communal recitation must be announced; and the four supports must be announced:
‘The going forth is dependent upon subsistence by alms-food.’”
In this regard, you should exert yourselves for as long as life lasts.
Additional gains include:
meals provided by the Sangha, designated meals, invitations, tickets for meals, fortnightly meals, Uposatha-day meals, and meals on the first day of the lunar fortnight.
The going forth is dependent upon rag-robe clothing.
In this regard, you should make an effort for as long as life lasts.
This is the extra gain:
There are robes made of linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and bark-fiber.
Renunciation is dependent upon the dwelling at the foot of a tree.
Therein, you must exert yourself for as long as life lasts.
Extra acquisitions:
a monastery, a gabled house, a mansion, a stilt house, and a cave.
Going forth by means of fermented urine as medicine.
In this regard, you should exert yourselves for as long as life lasts.
Any further gains are:
ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, and molasses.”
The four supports are finished.
65. The Four Things Not to Be Done.
Now at that time, having ordained a certain monk, the monks departed, leaving him all alone.
Thus, as he was coming along alone later on, he encountered his former wife on the road.
She said to him,
"Why have you now gone forth?"
“Yes, I have gone forth.
“Sexual intercourse is indeed rare for those who have gone forth;
come, practice sexual intercourse.”
Having engaged in sexual intercourse with her, he returned after a long time.
The bhikkhus said to him,
"Friend, why did you take so long?"
Then that bhikkhu reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"I allow you, bhikkhus, after having conferred full ordination, to give a companion and to explain the four things not to be done."
A fully ordained monk must not engage in sexual intercourse, even with an animal.

Any monk who engages in sexual intercourse is no longer an ascetic, no longer a son of the Sakyan. Just as a man whose head has been severed is incapable of living on by means of that bodily frame; so too, a monk who engages in sexual intercourse is no longer an ascetic, no longer a son of the Sakyan.
He is as one fallen from his status, defeated, no longer in communion. This is the first *pārājika* offense.
In the same way, a monk who has engaged in sexual intercourse is no longer a samaṇa, no longer a son of the Sakyans.
That must not be done by you for as long as life lasts.
A fully ordained monk must not take what is not given, which is reckoned as theft, even if it is only a blade of grass.
Whatever bhikkhu takes what has not been given, whether it be a pāda, the value of a pāda, or more than a pāda, in the manner of theft, he is no longer a samaṇa, no longer a son of the Sakyans.
Just as a withered leaf, once detached from its stalk, is incapable of becoming green again,
even so a bhikkhu who has taken what has not been given, whether it be a pāda, the value of a pāda, or more than a pāda, in the manner of theft, is no longer a samaṇa, no longer a son of the Sakyans.
That must not be done by you for as long as life lasts.
A bhikkhu who is fully ordained must not intentionally deprive any living being of life, even down to a worm or an ant.
Any bhikkhu who intentionally deprives a human being of life, even down to causing an abortion, is no longer a samaṇa, no longer a son of the Sakyan.
Just as a large stone, once split in two, cannot be joined back together,
even so a bhikkhu who intentionally deprives a human being of life is no longer a samaṇa, no longer a son of the Sakyans.
That must not be done by you for as long as life lasts.
A fully ordained monk must not boast of a superhuman state, even so much as saying, "I delight in solitude.

Any monk who, being of evil desire and driven by craving, boasts of a non-existent, unreal superhuman state—whether it be jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, the path, or the fruit—ceases to be a recluse and ceases to be a son of the Sakyan.
Just as a palmyra tree cut off at the crown is incapable of further growth, so too is such a person.
In the same way, a bhikkhu who has evil desires and is overcome by desire, having falsely claimed a non-existent, unreal superhuman state, becomes one who is not a recluse, not a son of the Sakyan.
That must not be done by you for as long as life lasts.
Thus end the four things that must not be done.
66. The Case of One Suspended for Not Seeing an Offense At that time, a certain monk who had been suspended for not seeing an offense disrobed.
Having returned again, he requested full ordination from the monks.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"In this case, monks, a monk who has been suspended for not seeing an offense disrobes.
Having returned again, he requests full ordination from the monks."
Thus he should be addressed:
"Will you see that offense? If he says, "I will see it," he may be ordained.
If [the candidate] says, "I will not see it," he should not be ordained.
Having ordained him, he should be asked:
"Will you see that offense?"
"If I shall see him, he may be ordained;
if I shall not see him, he must not be ordained.
Having ordained him, he should be told:
‘Will you see that offense?
If he says, ‘I will see it,’ he should be reinstated;
if he says, ‘I will not see it,’ he should not be reinstated.
Having restored him, he should be asked:
"Do you see that offense?
If he sees it, that is good.
If he does not see [the offense], he may be suspended again when a concordant assembly is available;
if a concordant assembly is not available, there is no offense in sharing or living together with him.
Furthermore, monks, here a monk who has been suspended for failure to make amends for an offense disrobes.
When he has returned again and requests full ordination from the monks,
he should be asked this:
“Will you make amends for that offense?”
If he says, "I will make amends," he should be ordained;
if he says, "I will not make amends," he should not be ordained.
Having ordained him, he should be told:
‘Will you make amends for that offense?
If he says, ‘I will make amends,’ he should be ordained;
if he says, ‘I will not make amends,’ he should not be ordained.
Having granted him full ordination, he should be asked:
"Will you confess that offense?
If he says, "I will confess it," he should be reinstated.
If he says, "I will not make amends," he is not to be reinstated.
Once reinstated, he should be told:
"Make amends for that offense."
If he makes amends, that is good.
If he does not make amends, he should be suspended again once a concordant assembly is obtained.
If a concordant assembly cannot be obtained, there is no offense in sharing communal life or dwelling together with him.
"But here, monks, a monk who has been suspended for not relinquishing an evil view goes forth into the lay life.
Having returned again, he requests full ordination from the monks.
He should be addressed as follows:"
‘Will you relinquish that evil view?
If he says, ‘I will relinquish it,’ he may be ordained;
if he says, ‘I will not relinquish it,’ he must not be ordained.
Having granted him the going-forth, he should be asked:
"Will you relinquish that evil view?
If he says, "I will relinquish it," he should be ordained.
If he says, "I will not relinquish it," he should not be ordained.
Once ordained, he should be asked:
"Will you relinquish that evil view?"
If he says, "I will relinquish it," he should be reinstated.
If he says, "I will not relinquish it," he should not be reinstated.
Having reinstated him, he should be told:
‘Relinquish that evil view.
If he relinquishes it, that is good.
If he does not relinquish it, then, while there is still a possibility of reconciliation, he should be suspended again.
“There is no offense in sharing or living together when harmony cannot be attained.
Thus ends the first Great Chapter.
Its summary:
In the Vinaya, which brings great benefit and bestows happiness upon those of virtuous conduct,
as well as in the discipline of those with evil desires who deserve restraint—
In modesty and in exertions,
in upholding the Dispensation,
and in the domain of the Omniscient Victor;
In the secure domain that is not another’s,
well-proclaimed and free from doubt,
in both the Khandhakas and the Vinaya.
And in his retinue and his motherland;
acting rightly according to the goal,
he practices with wisdom.
He who does not understand cattle does not protect the herd;
likewise, one who does not understand virtue—
Why should he maintain restraint?
Even when the Suttantas and the Abhidhamma have been forgotten;
When the Vinaya is not lost,
the Teaching remains;
therefore, for the sake of its compilation—
I shall proclaim the summary in due order,
according to my knowledge;
listen as I speak.
The basis, the origin, the offense,
the method, and the abbreviated repetition—
it is difficult to leave these out entirely.
"Know him by his guidance"— thus [it was said].
Bodhi, Rājāyatana,
Ajapāla, and Sahampati.
Brahmā Āḷāra and Udaka,
the bhikkhu and the seer Upaka;
Koṇḍañña, Vappa, and Bhaddiya.
Mahānāma and Assaji,
Yasa and the four and fifty—
all these he dispatched to the various directions.
The dwelling place, and thirty [disciples] were slain;
at Uruvelā, the three matted-hair ascetics;
the fire-chamber, and the great king.
Sakka, Brahmā, and Kevalā;
Paṃsukūla, Pokkharaṇī,
Silā, Kakudha, and Silā.
Bring the jambu, the mango,
the āmala, and the pāripuppha;
let them be split open and let them shine forth.
And let them go out, O Kassapa:
the cloud, the face, the staff,
and Māgadha have all sunk away.
Upatissa and Kolita, both well-known,
went forth; [the verses on] ill-clad [monks] and the expulsion.
The brahmin is emaciated and wretched;
he practices improper conduct,
as does the group of young men who fill their bellies.
Having departed with fools during the rains,
for ten years there was no formal support (nissaya).
They were not permitted to dismiss [the students].
The fool has five [types of] tranquility and six;
he who is another, and the naked one,
the one with unshorn matted hair, and the Śākya.
In Magadha there were five afflictions,
and one king with a finger;
and the King of Magadha gave his permission.
The prisoner, the one being whipped,
the one with marks, the debtor, the slave,
the one who broke his goods, Upāli, and the snake.
A faithful family, a thorn,
and indeed a dark place;
regarding the site, a boy, and training.
And why do they dwell thus?
Because everything depends upon the preceptor;
the thorn is in the act of provoking.
A paṇḍaka, one who has entered by theft,
a mother, and a father;
an arahant, a bhikkhunī, and one who causes schism.
And with blood as the seasoning.
Without a preceptor, by the Saṅgha,
a group, a paṇḍaka, and one who has been expelled;
The non-robes are those two;
and those three which are obtained by begging:
hands, feet, and both hands and feet.
Deafness, loss of the nose, or both;
fingerless hands, club feet, a withered arm,
being hunchbacked, and being dwarfed.
One with a goitre, one with the marks [of disease],
one with a whip, one with elephantiasis,
and one who corrupts the assembly with evil— these are the ones [to be avoided].
The one-eyed, the withered-limbed, and likewise the lame, the one afflicted by hemiplegia,
and the one whose modes of deportment are impaired.
One who is overcome by old age, mute, and deaf;
one who is blind and mute;
and that which is said to be blind and deaf.
And likewise one who is mute and deaf;
and one who is blind, mute, and deaf,
as well as dependence upon those who are shameless.
"One must dwell likewise for the duration [of the rains];
by one who requests, the characteristics [must be examined];
'Let him come,' they dispute."
With a single preceptor, Kassapa ordained [them].
They were seen to have received full ordination,
yet they were afflicted by illnesses.
The unadmonished wander on;
right there is the instruction.
And likewise, the fools [wander] even within the Saṅgha.
And not being authorized together;
the lifting up, the full ordination,
and the dependence— these three are each single.
In this Khandhaka, there are one hundred and seventy-two matters.
The Mahākhandhaka is concluded.
